T_retro.title: Retrospective analytic/continental division of pre-1931 philosophy (post-1945 historiographic projection)
T_retro.source_claim: The analytic/continental split as standardized only AFTER 1945 (Russell's 1945 'two schools' remark; the term 'continental philosophy' in its current sense widespread from the 1970s), projected retrospectively onto the sealed pre-1931 English-read corpus. Historiographic basis actually used: Glock 2008 'What is Analytic Philosophy?' (doi:10.1017/cbo9780511841125); Beaney ed. 2013 Oxford Handbook of the History of Analytic Philosophy, incl. Beaney 'The Historiography of Analytic Philosophy' (doi:10.1093/oxfordhb/9780199238842.013.0029); Soames 2003 Philosophical Analysis in the Twentieth Century vol.1 (doi:10.1515/9781400825790); Critchley 2001 Continental Philosophy: A Very Short Introduction as critical account (doi:10.1093/actrade/9780192853592.001.0001); Colapietro 2011 on intersecting pragmatist/analytic lineages (doi:10.1163/9789042033221_002); plus retrieved Wikipedia summaries of these accounts. CONSTRUCTIVIST CAVEAT: this division is a retrospective imposition - the object of study, not a natural kind; no corpus author self-identified with these labels.

Bergson.label: Continental (German idealism, Lebensphilosophie, existentialist antecedents, rejected Hegelian 'other')
Bergson.note: BORDERLINE, decided: standardly assigned to the continental Lebensphilosophie/process line (Deleuze's Le Bergsonisme revival, 1966); medium not high because the same source records he was 'influential in the traditions of analytic philosophy AND continental philosophy' - his early reception crossed the later split.

Bosanquet.label: Continental (German idealism, Lebensphilosophie, existentialist antecedents, rejected Hegelian 'other')
Bosanquet.note: BORDERLINE, decided: same status as Green - named leading figure of British idealism, the tradition whose rejection constitutes the analytic origin story; placed continental-side via the Hegelian lineage, contested because anglophone neo-Hegelians are not standardly claimed by continental historiography.

Comte.note: UNLABELLED, decided: the logical positivists borrowed the name 'positivism', but the standard analytic genealogies (Frege->Russell/Moore->Vienna Circle; Soames 2003; Beaney 2013) do not claim Comte as a movement precursor, and continental historiography (Critchley 2001) does not claim him either - his legacy forks into sociology. Could not be placed from sources consulted -> unlabelled rather than guessed. Untestable-as-null unit.

Croce.label: Continental (German idealism, Lebensphilosophie, existentialist antecedents, rejected Hegelian 'other')
Croce.note: BORDERLINE, decided: 'Italian idealist philosopher' in the neo-Hegelian historicist line, influential on Gramsci and Gentile; the idealist/historicist lineage falls inside continental historiography (German idealism and Hegelian views included per Continental philosophy wiki) and outside every analytic genealogy consulted.

Dewey.label: American pragmatism (contested third tradition - own class per planner directive)
Dewey.note: Same directive resolution as James: pragmatism as founding tradition (Peirce, James, Dewey, per Pragmatism wiki) is claimed as precursor by analytic-side genealogies and ignored by continental-side ones; contested third class rather than forced assimilation or null.

Eucken.label: Continental (German idealism, Lebensphilosophie, existentialist antecedents, rejected Hegelian 'other')
Eucken.note: BORDERLINE, decided: 1908 Nobel citation vindicates his 'idealistic philosophy of life' - Lebensphilosophie, a German continental current feeding existentialism; not claimed by any analytic genealogy consulted. Medium because he predates the canonical post-1945 continental movements (phenomenology, existentialism proper).

Green.label: Continental (German idealism, Lebensphilosophie, existentialist antecedents, rejected Hegelian 'other')
Green.note: BORDERLINE, decided: leading British idealist whose doctrines 'provoked ... Moore and Bertrand Russell to develop the ... methodology that gave rise to ... analytic philosophy' - he sits as the rejected Hegelian 'other' on the continental side of the retrospective split (continental philosophy includes Hegelian views); contested because continental historiography rarely claims anglophone idealists as its own.

Hegel.label: Continental (German idealism, Lebensphilosophie, existentialist antecedents, rejected Hegelian 'other')
Hegel.note: Continental philosophy 'includes German idealism ... as well as some Freudian, Hegelian, and Western Marxist views'; Critchley traces the continental line from Kant to German idealism (ch.2, doi:10.1093/actrade/9780192853592.003.0002). Hegel is also the constitutive rejected 'other' of analytic self-definition: 'Russell and Moore made a dismissal of Hegelianism ... a distinctive part of their new movement' (same source).

James.label: American pragmatism (contested third tradition - own class per planner directive)
James.note: DIRECTIVE RESOLVED as own class: analytic-side genealogies claim pragmatism as precursor (Mach 'a major influence on logical positivism and American pragmatism'; intersecting Dewey-Wittgenstein/Peirce-Wittgenstein lineages, Colapietro 2011 doi:10.1163/9789042033221_002), continental-side accounts (Critchley 2001) ignore them; the split does not cleanly place James. Own class keeps the unit testable rather than forfeiting it to null.

Kant.note: UNLABELLED, decided: common ancestor of BOTH retrospective lineages - continental historiography literally begins with him (Critchley ch.2 'Origins of Continental Philosophy: How to get from Kant to German Idealism'), while analytic genealogies run through Kantian problematics and neo-Kantian contexts (Frege/Carnap; Strawson's Kant). The split does not discriminate Kant; any one-sided label would misrepresent the sources. Untestable-as-null unit.

Kierkegaard.label: Continental (German idealism, Lebensphilosophie, existentialist antecedents, rejected Hegelian 'other')
Kierkegaard.note: Continental philosophy explicitly includes 'existentialism (and its antecedents, such as the thought of Kierkegaard and Nietzsche)'.

Mach.label: Analytic precursors (pre-movement figures claimed by analytic genealogies)
Mach.note: BORDERLINE, decided: 'As a philosopher of science, he was a major influence on logical positivism and American pragmatism'; the Anglo-Austrian precursor line is standard in analytic historiography (Dummett via Analytic philosophy wiki; Soames 2003 on the Vienna Circle). His pragmatist influence is noted but does not displace the analytic-side genealogical claim.

Mill.label: Analytic precursors (pre-movement figures claimed by analytic genealogies)
Mill.note: BORDERLINE, decided: Mill's 1840 Coleridge essay already contrasts 'Continental philosophy' with English Benthamite empiricism - the proto-drawing of the very line he is retrospectively placed on (empiricist side); empiricist-lineage analytic genealogies claim him (Glock 2008), and Ayer locates him in the empiricist option of the conventionalism debate (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conventionalism); British idealists defined themselves against Mill and Sidgwick (British idealism wiki).

Moore.label: Analytic (founders/core of the retrospective analytic tradition)
Moore.note: 'Doctrines of early British idealism provoked the Cambridge philosophers G. E. Moore and Bertrand Russell to develop the philosophical methodology that gave rise to a new philosophical tradition, analytic philosophy.'

Nietzsche.label: Continental (German idealism, Lebensphilosophie, existentialist antecedents, rejected Hegelian 'other')
Nietzsche.note: Named with Kierkegaard as antecedent of existentialism within the continental catch-all; central to Critchley's continental narrative, absent from analytic genealogies.

Peirce.label: American pragmatism (contested third tradition - own class per planner directive)
Peirce.note: Same directive resolution: the pragmatic maxim (1878) reads like a verificationist anticipation that analytic-side genealogies claim (Colapietro 2011 on Peirce-Wittgenstein intersecting lineages), while continental accounts pass him over; his scholastic-realist metaphysics fits neither canon -> contested pragmatism class.

Perry.label: Analytic precursors (pre-movement figures claimed by analytic genealogies)
Perry.note: BORDERLINE, decided: American new realism (incl. Perry) is 'often grouped with neutral monism or radical empiricism' and narrated as a program that 'declined as a dominant program in analytic philosophy' - i.e., historiography situates it inside the analytic story as part of the revolt against idealism; but Perry was also James's biographer-historian, so the pragmatist tie makes the placement contested.

Poincare.label: Analytic precursors (pre-movement figures claimed by analytic genealogies)
Poincare.note: BORDERLINE, decided: Poincare 'was among the first to articulate a conventionalist view' and 'Conventionalism was adopted by logical positivists, chiefly A. J. Ayer and Carl Hempel' - claimed by the analytic line through his philosophy-of-science reception; French, yet not claimed by continental historiography (Critchley's lineage runs Kant->German idealism->phenomenology). Medium: genealogies of the movement itself rarely name him.

Royce.label: Continental (German idealism, Lebensphilosophie, existentialist antecedents, rejected Hegelian 'other')
Royce.note: BORDERLINE, decided: 'American pragmatist and absolute idealist ... founder of American idealism', trained under Lotze in the German tradition; absolute idealism falls on the continental/Hegelian side of the retrospective split, but Royce is doubly peripheral (American; pragmatist-adjacent) -> contested.

Russell.label: Analytic (founders/core of the retrospective analytic tradition)
Russell.note: Named a central figure of analytic philosophy (with Frege, Moore, Wittgenstein); his alliance of logical analysis with natural science and 1945 'two schools' remark are the standard origin narrative (Soames 2003 vol.1 opens with Moore and Russell; Glock 2008).

Santayana.note: UNLABELLED, decided: neither lineage claims Santayana - analytic naturalists admire him, but his materialist Platonism, critical realism and literary-aphoristic mode fit neither post-1945 camp, and the sources consulted place him on no side of the division. Left unlabelled rather than guessed. Untestable-as-null unit.

Schopenhauer.label: Continental (German idealism, Lebensphilosophie, existentialist antecedents, rejected Hegelian 'other')
Schopenhauer.note: Philosophical pessimism is listed among the continental traditions, and the Schopenhauer->Nietzsche line is standard in continental historiography; absent from analytic genealogies (Soames 2003; Beaney 2013).

Sidgwick.label: Analytic precursors (pre-movement figures claimed by analytic genealogies)
Sidgwick.note: BORDERLINE, decided: Rawls called The Methods of Ethics the 'first truly academic work in moral theory, modern in both method and spirit' - the Cambridge empiricist/utilitarian line that later analytic ethics canonized; the British-idealist reaction grouped him with Mill as the empiricist 'other' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_idealism). Placed on the proto-analytic side at medium (not named in movement-origin genealogies themselves).

Spencer.note: UNLABELLED, decided: Victorian evolutionary synthetic philosophy; claimed by neither analytic nor continental genealogies in the division literature consulted - treated as pre-division Victorian thought (influencing pragmatists and positivists alike without belonging to either retrospective camp). Untestable-as-null unit.

Whitehead.label: Analytic (founders/core of the retrospective analytic tradition)
Whitehead.note: BORDERLINE, decided: co-author with Russell of Principia Mathematica, claimed by the logicist origin story of analytic historiography (Soames 2003); but his later process metaphysics 'radically departed from most of Western philosophy' and lives outside the analytic canon (resonating with Bergson/Deleuze). Dual legacy -> contested analytic.

T_translated.title: Surface-form confound control: original English vs translated into English
T_translated.source_claim: Proposed by the PHASE 2 sealed-reader dispatch (2026-10-03) as a non-doctrinal translationese confound control for the 25-author Project Gutenberg pre-1931 English corpus; class assignment is by the original language of each author's listed corpus works, not by philosophical school.

Bergson.label: Translated
Bergson.note: French philosopher; Time and Free Will (Essai sur les donnees immediates de la conscience) and Creative Evolution (L'Evolution creatrice) are French originals read in English translation.

Bosanquet.label: OriginalEnglish
Bosanquet.note: English philosopher; both listed logic and political-philosophy works are English originals.

Comte.label: Translated
Comte.note: French philosopher; A General View of Positivism is an English translation of the French original.

Croce.label: Translated
Croce.note: Italian philosopher; Aesthetic, Logic, and Philosophy of the Practical are Italian originals in English translation.

Dewey.label: OriginalEnglish
Dewey.note: American philosopher; all four listed works are English originals.

Eucken.label: Translated
Eucken.note: German philosopher; Life's Basis and Life's Ideal and Ethics and Modern Thought are German originals in English translation.

Green.label: OriginalEnglish
Green.note: English philosopher; Lectures on the Principles of Political Obligation were delivered and published in English.

Hegel.label: Translated
Hegel.note: German philosopher; The Logic of Hegel and Philosophy of Mind are Wallace translations of the Encyclopaedia Logic and Philosophy of Mind.

James.label: OriginalEnglish
James.note: American philosopher; all four listed works, including Essays in Radical Empiricism, are English originals.

Kant.label: Translated
Kant.note: German philosopher; Critique of Pure Reason, Prolegomena, and the Groundwork (Fundamental Principles...) are German originals in English translation.

Kierkegaard.label: Translated
Kierkegaard.note: Danish philosopher who wrote in Danish; Selections from the Writings is an English translation.

Mach.label: Translated
Mach.note: Austrian physicist/philosopher writing in German; Popular Scientific Lectures is translated from the German.

Mill.label: OriginalEnglish
Mill.note: English philosopher; Utilitarianism, A System of Logic, and Auguste Comte and Positivism are English originals.

Moore.label: OriginalEnglish
Moore.note: English philosopher; Principia Ethica and Philosophical Studies written in English.

Nietzsche.label: Translated
Nietzsche.note: German philosopher; all four listed works are German originals read in English translation.

Peirce.label: OriginalEnglish
Peirce.note: American philosopher/logician; Chance, Love, and Logic is an English-language collection of his English writings.

Perry.label: OriginalEnglish
Perry.note: American philosopher; both listed works are English originals.

Poincare.label: Translated
Poincare.note: French mathematician/philosopher; The Foundations of Science is an English translation of French originals.

Royce.label: OriginalEnglish
Royce.note: American philosopher; The Sources of Religious Insight is an English original.

Russell.label: OriginalEnglish
Russell.note: English philosopher; all four listed works were written and published in English.

Santayana.label: OriginalEnglish
Santayana.note: Spanish-born American philosopher; The Life of Reason was published in English, and the listed works are English originals despite his Spanish birth.

Schopenhauer.label: Translated
Schopenhauer.note: German philosopher; World as Will and Idea, Studies in Pessimism (translated essays), and The Basis of Morality are all German originals.

Sidgwick.label: OriginalEnglish
Sidgwick.note: English philosopher; The Methods of Ethics is an English original.

Spencer.label: OriginalEnglish
Spencer.note: English philosopher; First Principles and The Data of Ethics are English originals.

Whitehead.label: OriginalEnglish
Whitehead.note: English mathematician/philosopher; The Concept of Nature and Science and the Modern World are English originals.

era.title: Composition-date era taxonomy (rival to inherited six schools)
era.source_claim: Proposed by the Six Schools Lab advocate, 2026-10-03, in this dispatch conversation, as a rival hypothesis to the inherited six-schools taxonomy. Era boundaries follow standard periodizations of early Chinese intellectual history; per-book datings follow standard reference scholarship of the type surveyed in Michael Loewe (ed.), Early Chinese Texts: A Bibliographical Guide (1993), with later specialist studies including Brooks & Brooks, The Original Analects (1998), Yuri Pines, 'Dating a Pre-Imperial Text: The Case Study of the Book of Lord Shang' (2016), and the cited reference articles. CODEBOOK RULE (pre-registered): layered/compilatory texts (Analects, Liji, Guanzi, Kongzi Jiayu, Zhongyong, Liezi, Guiguzi) are assigned by the date of final compilation/redaction of the RECEIVED text as reported by the cited reference, not by their earliest stratum; where cited scholarship genuinely diverges, the assignment is marked contested. Sealed excavated units (Huangdi_Sijing, Sun_Bin_Bingfa) are never labeled.

Analects.label: Qin-Han (221 BCE-220 CE)
Analects.note: Layered text; codebook rule = final compilation. Cited source: large portions Warring States, but the work 'achieved its final form during the mid-Han dynasty'. Brooks & Brooks would place completion in the late Warring States (~315 BCE), so era assignment is contested.

Gongsun_Longzi.label: Late Warring States (c. 350-221 BCE)
Gongsun_Longzi.note: Anthology of works of Gongsun Long (c. 320-250 BCE); six of fourteen original essays survive, so integrity/dating are somewhat uncertain.

Guanzi.label: Qin-Han (221 BCE-220 CE)
Guanzi.note: Layered compilation; codebook rule = final compilation. Received Guanzi edited by Liu Xiang c. 26 BCE from material of many authors (4th c. BCE onward); Sato and Rickett disagree over whether some chapters are Han.

Guiguzi.label: Qin-Han (221 BCE-220 CE)
Guiguzi.note: Layered compilation; codebook rule = final compilation. Cited source: compiled between the late Warring States period and the end of the Han dynasty, and book III is likely a later addition; genuine Warring States rhetorical corpus underlies it.

Han_Feizi.label: Late Warring States (c. 350-221 BCE)
Han_Feizi.note: Most chapters date to the mid-3rd century BCE (Han Fei d. 233 BCE); later Laozi-commentary chapters are addenda.

Huainanzi.label: Qin-Han (221 BCE-220 CE)
Huainanzi.note: Essays from debates at the court of Liu An, presented to Emperor Wu before 139 BCE.

Huangdi_Sijing.note: SEALED excavated manuscript; never labeled or used in this taxonomy.

Kongzi_Jiayu.label: Post-Han (c. 220-420 CE)
Kongzi_Jiayu.note: Layered text; codebook rule = final compilation. Received text associated with Cao Wei scholar Wang Su (195-256 CE); Han tomb finds at Dingzhou and Shuanggudui complicate the old 'forgery' verdict, and earlier Han versions existed.

Laozi.label: Late Warring States (c. 350-221 BCE)
Laozi.note: Guodian slips (c. 300 BCE) attest early Laozi-like bundles that were not yet a unified text; a conservative estimate dates the consolidated text to the mid-3rd century BCE, consolidating older sayings.

Liezi.label: Post-Han (c. 220-420 CE)
Liezi.note: Layered text; codebook rule = final compilation. Received text compiled around the 4th century CE by Zhang Zhan (fl. c. 370 CE); Han-era references and Liu Xiang's edition attest an earlier related work.

Liji.label: Qin-Han (221 BCE-220 CE)
Liji.note: Layered compilation; codebook rule = final compilation. Diverse Warring States and early Han materials compiled in the Han (title associated with Han scholar Dai Sheng); individual chapter datings remain debated.

Liutao.label: Late Warring States (c. 350-221 BCE)
Liutao.note: Cited source: modern historians nominally date final composition to the Warring States period (475-221 BCE) while some see Han-era material; assigned to the later part of that span, contested.

Lushi_Chunqiu.label: Late Warring States (c. 350-221 BCE)
Lushi_Chunqiu.note: Compiled c. 239 BCE under Lü Buwei, with completion possibly stretching to just after his death (235 BCE).

Mencius.label: Late Warring States (c. 350-221 BCE)
Mencius.note: Cited source: written during the late 4th century BCE, largely by Mencius's disciples; Mencius d. c. 289 BCE.

Mozi.label: Late Warring States (c. 350-221 BCE)
Mozi.note: Layered anthology: early chapters derive from the 5th-century-BCE Mozi, but the dialectical chapters are a later 3rd-century-BCE development; codebook rule places the compilation horizon in the late Warring States.

Shangjunshu.label: Late Warring States (c. 350-221 BCE)
Shangjunshu.note: Pines (2016) shows a 3rd-century-BCE core under Shang Yang's name but argues the book took over a century to write, remaining a pre-imperial Warring States compilation.

Sima_Fa.label: Early and mid Warring States (c. 480-350 BCE)
Sima_Fa.note: Developed in Qi during the 4th century BCE, mid-Warring States period; falls at the boundary of the two Warring States eras.

Sun_Bin_Bingfa.note: SEALED excavated manuscript; never labeled or used in this taxonomy.

Sunzi_Bingfa.label: Early and mid Warring States (c. 480-350 BCE)
Sunzi_Bingfa.note: Cited source: dating from roughly the late Spring and Autumn period (5th century BCE); earliest parts probably postdate the 6th-century-BCE Sun Tzu by at least a century. Some scholarship pushes portions later.

Wei_Liaozi.label: Late Warring States (c. 350-221 BCE)
Wei_Liaozi.note: Warring States text; present form assumed around the end of the 4th century BCE.

Wuzi.label: Early and mid Warring States (c. 480-350 BCE)
Wuzi.note: Core nominally composed around Wu Qi's lifetime (440-381 BCE), mid-Warring States; cited source states there is no consensus on the latest date of final composition.

Xiaojing.label: Late Warring States (c. 350-221 BCE)
Xiaojing.note: Cited source: 'most likely written during the late Warring States period and early Han dynasty', dated 4th-3rd century BCE; the span straddles the era boundary, so assignment is contested.

Xunzi.label: Late Warring States (c. 350-221 BCE)
Xunzi.note: Core essays attributed to Xun Kuang, a 3rd-century BCE philosopher; later 1st-century-CE recension by Liu Xiang treated as transmission, not composition horizon.

Zhongyong.label: Qin-Han (221 BCE-220 CE)
Zhongyong.note: Layered text; codebook rule = final compilation. Traditional attribution to Zisi doubted since Cui Shu; some modern scholars hold parts were written or edited at the Qin-Han transition, while a Warring States dating is also defended.

Zhuangzi.label: Late Warring States (c. 350-221 BCE)
Zhuangzi.note: Cited source: written during the late Warring States period; outer and mixed layers continued to accrete into the Han before the later Guo Xiang recension.

genre.title: Genre / literary-form taxonomy of transmitted early Chinese texts (H-C1 rival confound control)
genre.source_claim: Proposed by Six Schools Lab Advocate A on 2026-10-03 in this dispatch conversation, as the H-C1 rival/confound control to the inherited six-schools taxonomy: every transmitted book is labelled by its dominant received literary form, never by doctrine or 'school'. The class set and assignments follow standard reference scholarship on early Chinese text types: Loewe (ed.), Early Chinese Texts: A Bibliographical Guide (1993); Mark Edward Lewis, Writing and Authority in Early China (1999) (genre spectrum from recorded speech/anecdote through persuasion and the argumentative essay to canonical verse); Nylan & Csikszentmihalyi on compilation practice and 'Analects'-type text formation (Csikszentmihalyi, Material Virtue, 2006; Nylan & Csikszentmihalyi, T'oung Pao 89, 2003); Ralph D. Sawyer, The Seven Military Classics of Ancient China (1993) on bing-jia literature as a literary form; Victor Mair, Tao Te Ching (1990) on the Laozi as rhymed philosophical verse; A.C. Graham, The Book of Lieh-tzu (1960/1990) on anecdote-driven prose; Yuri Pines, Early China 39 (2016) and The Book of Lord Shang (2017) on treatise-essay compilation; John S. Major et al., The Huainanzi (2010) on the compendium/summa form; Knoblock & Riegel, The Annals of Lu Buwei (2000) on the planned encyclopedic compilation; Allyn Rickett, Guanzi (1985/1998); Andrew Plaks, The Four Books (2003) on treatise vs recorded-discourse forms. CODEBOOK RULES (pre-registered): (1) assign the form that characterizes the majority of the received text's bulk and rhetorical mode; (2) functional genre overrides framing - a dialogue-framed military manual (Wuzi, Liutao) remains a bing-jia treatise; (3) multi-author, redactor-shaped collections (Guanzi, Liji, Lushi Chunqiu, Huainanzi) take the encyclopedic-compilation class; (4) where a text genuinely balances incompatible forms (Mozi, Zhuangzi, Guiguzi) or is so layered that single-form assignment is unstable (Guanzi, Liji, Huainanzi), the assignment is marked contested; (5) the two sealed excavated units (Huangdi_Sijing, Sun_Bin_Bingfa) are never labelled. NOTE ON CITATIONS: OpenAlex search was unavailable throughout this session (persistent HTTP 429), so citation fields use verified reference-article URLs (the convention used in the lab's already-frozen 'era' and 'region' taxonomies) plus one verified DOI (Pines 2016); the full scholarly works relied on are named in this source_claim and in each per-book note.

Analects.label: Analects-type sayings and lore collections (yu-lun ti)
Analects.note: Short recorded sayings and conversations of Confucius and disciples, collected and edited by followers (Ban Gu, Hanshu); the paradigmatic analects-type (yu/lun-ji) collection. Csikszentmihalyi 2006 on 'Analects'-type texts; Lewis 1999 on recorded speech as a genre; Loewe (ed.) 1993.

Gongsun_Longzi.label: Thematic argumentative treatises (lun-type essays)
Gongsun_Longzi.note: Short dialectical argumentative essays in bian-disputation form ('Bai ma lun' and companions); survives as a 6-piece anthology of once-14 pieces with heavy corruption - form clear, integrity uncertain, hence medium. Graham, Studies in Chinese Philosophy and Logicians; Loewe (ed.) 1993.

Guanzi.label: Encyclopedic compilations and composite summae
Guanzi.note: Anonymous multi-author corpus (76 surviving of 86 chapters) of material spanning centuries, edited by Liu Xiang c. 26 BCE: mixes dialogue chapters, essays, technical economic/administrative chapters and verse-like passages; compilation class fits the redacted received whole, but the internal heterogeneity makes any single-form assignment contested. Rickett 1985/98; Loewe (ed.) 1993; Sato on its composition.

Guiguzi.label: Thematic argumentative treatises (lun-type essays)
Guiguzi.note: Manual of persuasion technique (zong-heng rhetoric): short chapters of technical instruction with appended commentary layers, compiled between late Warring States and end of Han, book III a later addition; whether the received whole is a technical treatise manual or a layered compilation is genuinely open - contested. Loewe (ed.) 1993.

Han_Feizi.label: Thematic argumentative treatises (lun-type essays)
Han_Feizi.note: Core is systematic argumentative essays of statecraft theory ('Wu du', 'Ding fa'), but the anthology also holds persuasion-anecdote corpora ('Shui lin', 'Shui nan') and Laozi-commentary chapters ('Jie Lao', 'Yu Lao'); treatise core dominant, heterogeneity flagged via medium. Loewe (ed.) 1993; A.C. Graham on Han Fei as synthesizer; Goldin on Han Fei's essays.

Huainanzi.label: Encyclopedic compilations and composite summae
Huainanzi.note: Twenty-one-essay compendium 'compiled as a compendium for an enlightened sovereign' at Liu An's court (before 139 BCE), synthesizing many traditions (Major et al. 2010). It sits between a planned systematic summa (like Lushi Chunqiu) and a loose compilation, and its essays are themselves rhetorically lush - hence compilation class, contested. Loewe (ed.) 1993.

Huangdi_Sijing.note: SEALED excavated manuscript (Mawangdui silk texts, buried 168 BCE); intentionally not labelled or used in this taxonomy.

Kongzi_Jiayu.label: Analects-type sayings and lore collections (yu-lun ti)
Kongzi_Jiayu.note: Self-described supplement to the Analects: Confucius lore - recorded sayings, conversations and anecdotes - compiled from disciple records (received Wang Su recension). Genre unambiguous; medium only because it expands toward biographical narrative. Loewe (ed.) 1993; Csikszentmihalyi 2006; Nylan & Csikszentmihalyi 2003 on compilation practice.

Laozi.label: Verse and aphoristic philosophical poetry
Laozi.note: 81 short chapters of rhymed aphoristic verse - philosophical poetry, categorically distinct from the discursive prose genres; its 'poetic' character is noted even in comparison with other Daoist texts. Mair 1990 (verse-oriented translation and introduction); Lewis 1999 on canonical verse; Loewe (ed.) 1993.

Liezi.label: Dialogue- and parable-driven philosophical prose
Liezi.note: Anecdote- and fable-driven prose: chapters are chains of narrative and dialogue episodes rather than exposition (Graham, The Book of Lieh-tzu, 1960/1990). Medium because the received text is a layered compilation (Zhang Zhan recension, c. 4th c. CE).

Liji.label: Encyclopedic compilations and composite summae
Liji.note: 49-chapter heterogeneous compilation of ritual records, expositions, dialogues and essays, lacking consistent structure (Riegel, 'Li ji', in Loewe (ed.) 1993; Nylan 2001). Compilation class, contested because whole chapters are strongly generic in different ways (treatise-like Zhongyong/Daxue, anecdote-dialogue like Tan Gong).

Liutao.label: Military treatises (bing-jia literature)
Liutao.note: 'Treatise on civil and military strategy' among the Seven Military Classics, cast as instruction dictated by Jiang Ziya to King Wen; bing-jia genre clear, medium because of heavy dialogue framing and uncertain (likely late) composition. Sawyer 1993; Loewe (ed.) 1993.

Lushi_Chunqiu.label: Encyclopedic compilations and composite summae
Lushi_Chunqiu.note: Planned encyclopedic compilation produced by design under Lu Buwei (c. 239 BCE) with tripartite ji/lun/lan architecture; Loewe: 'unique among early works in that it is well organized and comprehensive'. Knoblock & Riegel 2000; Loewe (ed.) 1993.

Mencius.label: Dialogue- and parable-driven philosophical prose
Mencius.note: Extended master-disciple dialogues and set-piece debates compiled by disciples; the classic dialogical philosophical prose bridging analects-type records and the treatise. Plaks 2003; Lewis 1999; Loewe (ed.) 1993.

Mozi.label: Thematic argumentative treatises (lun-type essays)
Mozi.note: Received text mixes four distinct forms: doctrinal essay triads (treatise core, the bulk), dialectical 'canon' chapters, narrative-dialogue sections, and defensive-siege technical manuals; no single form dominates the whole, so the treatise-plurality assignment is contested. Loewe (ed.) 1993; Fraser on Mohist dialectics; Lewis 1999.

Shangjunshu.label: Thematic argumentative treatises (lun-type essays)
Shangjunshu.note: Policy-argument essays with a few dialogic frames; Pines (2016, Early China 39; and The Book of Lord Shang, 2017) shows multi-author treatise-style chapters accruing over a century - treatise-dominant but layered, hence medium.

Sima_Fa.label: Military treatises (bing-jia literature)
Sima_Fa.note: Short bing-jia text on military regulations and administration preserving fragments of older ritual-warfare lore; received form is a military treatise. Sawyer 1993; Loewe (ed.) 1993.

Sun_Bin_Bingfa.note: SEALED excavated manuscript (Yinqueshan bamboo slips); intentionally not labelled or used in this taxonomy.

Sunzi_Bingfa.label: Military treatises (bing-jia literature)
Sunzi_Bingfa.note: Canonical bing-jia manual: terse topical chapters of strategic doctrine with minimal framing; listed among the Seven Military Classics. Sawyer 1993; Loewe (ed.) 1993.

Wei_Liaozi.label: Military treatises (bing-jia literature)
Wei_Liaozi.note: Military treatise combining dialogic audience chapters (King Hui of Liang) with expository chapters on command, discipline and civil-military organization; two same-titled works existed in Han catalogues, so integrity is uncertain - medium. Sawyer 1993; Loewe (ed.) 1993.

Wuzi.label: Military treatises (bing-jia literature)
Wuzi.note: One of the Seven Military Classics; six topical chapters of military doctrine cast as dialogue between Wu Qi and Marquis Wen of Wei - the dialogue frame does not override the functional genre (codebook rule 2). Sawyer 1993.

Xiaojing.label: Analects-type sayings and lore collections (yu-lun ti)
Xiaojing.note: Brief classic framed as recorded conversation between Confucius and Zengzi; dominant form is recorded discourse, not sustained exposition - hence sayings class, with medium confidence because its headed chapters show quasi-treatise organization. Loewe (ed.) 1993; Nylan 2001 on canon formation.

Xunzi.label: Thematic argumentative treatises (lun-type essays)
Xunzi.note: Sustained titled argumentative essays - the first mature philosophical treatises in Chinese (lun-type discourse). Knoblock 1988-94; Loewe (ed.) 1993; Lewis 1999 on the rise of the essay.

Zhongyong.label: Thematic argumentative treatises (lun-type essays)
Zhongyong.note: Originally a Liji chapter; the received work is a coherent expository treatise on zhong/yong and self-cultivation (Plaks 2003 treats it as essay-type). Medium because its layered composition has been debated since Cui Shu.

Zhuangzi.label: Dialogue- and parable-driven philosophical prose
Zhuangzi.note: Dominant mode is parable, anecdote and imaginary dialogue (yu-yan, 'goblet words'), but the received 33-chapter text is a layered compilation (Inner/Outer/Miscellaneous) that also contains argumentative essays; genuinely mixed form, hence contested. Loewe (ed.) 1993; Graham's chapter studies; Lewis 1999.

hanshu_catalog.title: Hanshu Yiwenzhi bibliographic-shelf taxonomy
hanshu_catalog.source_claim: The partition is the bibliographic scheme of the Yiwenzhi treatise in Ban Gu, Ban Zhao, and Ban Biao's Book of Han (finished 111 CE), itself based on Liu Xin's earlier imperial catalogue. It sorts learning into Six-Arts, Masters, poetry, military, technical, and medical shelves; for this corpus the operative shelves are Six-Arts, the Masters' schools (Confucian, Daoist, Legalist, Names, Mohist, Diplomats, Miscellaneous/Syncretist, etc.), and Military literature. Modern scholarship on retrospective jia construction (e.g. Smith 2003; Csikszentmihalyi and Nylan 2003) is the reason categories are treated as a historical bibliographic hypothesis, not discovered intellectual essence. Source URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Han. Pre-registered codebook: (1) assign each transmitted book to the Yiwenzhi shelf on which its title or direct Han catalogue ancestor appears; (2) label the whole book, not individual layers, because the unit is book-level; (3) preserve the Han catalogue's distinction between Six-Arts, Masters, and Military shelves rather than collapsing them into Sima Tan's six schools; (4) if the source catalogue omits or ambiguously identifies a transmitted title, use the nearest category explicitly supplied by cited scholarship and lower confidence; (5) mark contested whenever later bibliography or modern scholarship assigns the same book to another category; (6) the two sealed excavated units are always null.

Analects.label: Six-Arts (Han ritual/classical canon)
Analects.note: The Yiwenzhi places Lunyu in its Six-Arts/Lunyu subsection; the page describes its early-Han status as a commentary on the Five Classics and central Confucian text.

Gongsun_Longzi.label: School of Names (Mingjia)
Gongsun_Longzi.note: The Yiwenzhi lists Gongsun Longzi under Mingjia; the page identifies Gongsun Long and his anthology with the School of Names.

Guanzi.label: Daoist Masters (Daojia)
Guanzi.note: The Yiwenzhi lists Guanzi under Daojia, while the Sui catalogue moved it to Fajia; the page describes both placements and mixed Legalist/Daoist/Confucian content.

Guiguzi.label: Diplomat Masters (Zonghengjia)
Guiguzi.note: The transmitted Guiguzi is absent from the operative Yiwenzhi list, so the ambiguity rule uses its cited identification as a representative Zongheng work; later bibliography could class it as Zajia, hence contested.

Han_Feizi.label: Legalist Masters (Fajia)
Han_Feizi.note: The Yiwenzhi lists Hanzi under Fajia; the page describes essays in the Legalist tradition.

Huainanzi.label: Miscellaneous/Syncretist Masters (Zajia)
Huainanzi.note: Confucian bibliographers classified Huainanzi as Zajia/Syncretist, but it later came to be treated as a Daoist work; the page records both traditions.

Huangdi_Sijing.note: Sealed excavated manuscript; intentionally not labelled and not used to set any transmitted assignment.

Kongzi_Jiayu.label: Six-Arts (Han ritual/classical canon)
Kongzi_Jiayu.note: The Yiwenzhi lists Kongzi Jiayu with the Lunyu group; the page confirms this first-century listing but stresses the disputed later formation of the received text.

Laozi.label: Daoist Masters (Daojia)
Laozi.note: The Yiwenzhi places Laozi materials under Daojia; the page calls the text foundational for Taoism.

Liezi.label: Daoist Masters (Daojia)
Liezi.note: The Yiwenzhi lists Liezi in eight pian under Daojia; the page also notes scholarly argument that the received compilation is much later.

Liji.label: Six-Arts (Han ritual/classical canon)
Liji.note: The Yiwenzhi Li subsection includes the Records; the page calls Liji part of the ritual component of the Confucian Five Classics, while its layers are diverse and unevenly dated.

Liutao.label: Confucian Masters (Rujia)
Liutao.note: Yiwenzhi lists Zhou Shi Liu Tao under Rujia, so the exact-catalogue rule controls despite the later Seven Military Classics classification; the transmitted formation and Taigong associations remain disputed.

Lushi_Chunqiu.label: Miscellaneous/Syncretist Masters (Zajia)
Lushi_Chunqiu.note: The Yiwenzhi lists Lüshi Chunqiu under Zajia; the page says it was traditionally classified as Syncretist because it combines many schools.

Mencius.label: Confucian Masters (Rujia)
Mencius.note: The Yiwenzhi lists Mengzi under Rujia; the page identifies the anthology with the Confucian philosopher Mencius.

Mozi.label: Mohist Masters (Mojia)
Mozi.note: The Yiwenzhi lists Mozi under Mojia; the page describes the book as expounding Mohism.

Shangjunshu.label: Legalist Masters (Fajia)
Shangjunshu.note: The Yiwenzhi lists Shangjun in Fajia, but also lists a separate 27-pian Gongsun Yang work among military strategists; the layered transmission makes the book/ancestor mapping contested.

Sima_Fa.label: Six-Arts (Han ritual/classical canon)
Sima_Fa.note: Yiwenzhi puts Military Rites Sima Fa under Li, and the page says Ban Gu classified it as concerning rites and propriety; later tradition makes it a military classic, so the category conflict is flagged.

Sun_Bin_Bingfa.note: Sealed excavated manuscript; intentionally not labelled and not used to set any transmitted assignment.

Sunzi_Bingfa.label: Military literature (Bingshu)
Sunzi_Bingfa.note: The Yiwenzhi military-strategies subsection lists Wu Sunzi's military text; the page identifies the work as an ancient Chinese military treatise.

Wei_Liaozi.label: Miscellaneous/Syncretist Masters (Zajia)
Wei_Liaozi.note: Yiwenzhi lists Wei Liaozi under Zajia, whereas the received text is now one of the Seven Military Classics and has Legalist affinities; the page notes two same-titled Han works.

Wuzi.label: Military literature (Bingshu)
Wuzi.note: The Yiwenzhi military-strategies subsection lists Wu Qi; the page identifies Wuzi as one of China's Seven Military Classics.

Xiaojing.label: Six-Arts (Han ritual/classical canon)
Xiaojing.note: The Yiwenzhi has a Xiaojing subsection within Six-Arts; the page identifies it as a Confucian classic.

Xunzi.label: Confucian Masters (Rujia)
Xunzi.note: The Yiwenzhi lists Sun Qingzi under Rujia; the page associates Xunzi with the Confucian tradition.

Zhongyong.label: Six-Arts (Han ritual/classical canon)
Zhongyong.note: The Yiwenzhi Li subsection contains a Zhongyong treatise; the page says the transmitted Zhongyong was originally a chapter of the Book of Rites, although authorship and dating are controversial.

Zhuangzi.label: Daoist Masters (Daojia)
Zhuangzi.note: The Yiwenzhi lists Zhuangzi under Daojia; the page identifies it as a foundational Taoist text.

hanshu_yiwenzhi.title: Hanshu Yiwenzhi bibliographic taxonomy (Liu Xin/Ban Gu ten Masters schools plus Six Arts and Military Books)
hanshu_yiwenzhi.source_claim: Proposed by the imperial-library bibliography underlying Ban Gu's Hanshu 'Yiwenzhi' (early 2nd century CE), itself based on Liu Xin's lost Qilüe; it is a historical catalogue placement, not a modern claim about doctrinal essence. Codebook/attribution rule: (1) explicit or title-equivalent Hanshu placement controls; (2) a transmitted component chapter inherits its container's placement; (3) titles absent from the Yiwenzhi, or with conflicting/duplicate Han entries, receive the best-attested placement but are marked contested; (4) the sealed excavated units are null. Sources for the partition: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liu_Xin_(scholar), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Han, and Michael Hunter, 'Yiwen zhi Bibliography in Its Own Context' (2019), https://doi.org/10.7817/jameroriesoci.138.4.0763.

Analects.label: Six Arts (Liu yi): Confucian classics
Analects.note: Hanshu 30 places Lunyu under Six Arts > Lunyu; the cited page notes its early-Han status as a Five Classics commentary.

Gongsun_Longzi.label: Masters: Names (Mingjia)
Gongsun_Longzi.note: Hanshu 30 lists Gongsun Longzi, 14 pian, under Mingjia; cited page identifies Gongsun Long and his collected works with the School of Names.

Guanzi.label: Masters: Daoist (Daojia)
Guanzi.note: Hanshu 30 lists Guanzi, 86 pian, under Daojia; cited page records this placement and the later Sui reclassification as Legalist. Historical-catalogue rule keeps Daojia.

Guiguzi.label: Masters: Diplomatist (Zonghengjia)
Guiguzi.note: No explicit Guiguzi entry survives in the Yiwenzhi's Zonghengjia list. Assigned by its well-attested rhetoric/persuasion and School-of-Diplomacy association, but absence from the Han catalogue makes the mapping contested.

Han_Feizi.label: Masters: Legalist (Fajia)
Han_Feizi.note: Hanshu 30 lists Hanzi, 55 pian, under Fajia; cited page confirms the 55-chapter Hanshu catalogue listing and Legalist affiliation.

Huainanzi.label: Masters: Syncretist (Zajia)
Huainanzi.note: Hanshu 30 lists Huainan nei and wai under Zajia; cited page notes Confucian bibliographers classified it as Zajia.

Huangdi_Sijing.note: Sealed excavated unit; protocol forbids labelling.

Kongzi_Jiayu.label: Six Arts (Liu yi): Confucian classics
Kongzi_Jiayu.note: Hanshu 30 lists Kongzi Jiayu, 27 juan, in the Lunyu subdivision of Six Arts; cited page confirms the Yiwenzhi listing.

Laozi.label: Masters: Daoist (Daojia)
Laozi.note: Hanshu 30 lists Laozi transmission literature under Daojia; cited page identifies the Laozi as the foundational Daoist text.

Liezi.label: Masters: Daoist (Daojia)
Liezi.note: Hanshu 30 lists Liezi, 8 pian, under Daojia; cited page reports that Book of Han bibliography entry.

Liji.label: Six Arts (Liu yi): Confucian classics
Liji.note: The Records (ji), 131 pian, are placed under Six Arts > Rites; the cited page identifies Liji as a Confucian classic.

Liutao.label: Masters: Daoist (Daojia)
Liutao.note: The Yiwenzhi has no exact received-Liutao entry, but places Taigong, 237 pian (including bing works), under Daojia. Because the relation of that composite entry to the received Six Secret Teachings is inferential, the assignment is contested.

Lushi_Chunqiu.label: Masters: Syncretist (Zajia)
Lushi_Chunqiu.note: Hanshu 30 lists Lüshi Chunqiu, 26 pian, under Zajia; cited page notes traditional Syncretist classification.

Mencius.label: Masters: Confucian (Rujia)
Mencius.note: Hanshu 30 lists Mengzi, 11 pian, under Rujia; the cited page identifies the anthology as Confucian.

Mozi.label: Masters: Mohist (Mojia)
Mozi.note: Hanshu 30 lists Mozi, 71 pian, under Mojia; cited page identifies the book with Mohism.

Shangjunshu.label: Masters: Legalist (Fajia)
Shangjunshu.note: Hanshu 30 lists Shang jun, 29 pian, under Fajia; cited page confirms that listing, while noting a separate Gongsun Yang military entry.

Sima_Fa.label: Six Arts (Liu yi): Confucian classics
Sima_Fa.note: Hanshu 30 places Military Rites Sima Fa, 155 pian, under Six Arts > Rites; cited page explicitly notes Ban Gu's rites classification.

Sun_Bin_Bingfa.note: Sealed excavated unit; protocol forbids labelling.

Sunzi_Bingfa.label: Military Books (Bingshu)
Sunzi_Bingfa.note: Hanshu 30 places Wu Sunzi bingfa, 82 pian, under Bing shu > strategic planning (quanmou).

Wei_Liaozi.label: Masters: Syncretist (Zajia)
Wei_Liaozi.note: Hanshu 30 lists Weiliaozi, 29 pian, under Zajia, but also a separate Weiliao, 31 pian, under Military Books > situations. Cited page confirms two same-name Han works; exact identity of the received text is disputed, so Zajia is retained as the title-equivalent placement.

Wuzi.label: Military Books (Bingshu)
Wuzi.note: Hanshu 30 lists Wu Qi, 48 pian, under Bing shu > strategic planning; cited page identifies Wuzi as a military-strategy classic.

Xiaojing.label: Six Arts (Liu yi): Confucian classics
Xiaojing.note: Hanshu 30 has a Xiaojing subdivision under Six Arts; the cited page identifies it as a Confucian classic.

Xunzi.label: Masters: Confucian (Rujia)
Xunzi.note: Hanshu 30 lists Sunqingzi, 33 pian, under Rujia; the cited page associates Xunzi with the Confucian tradition.

Zhongyong.label: Six Arts (Liu yi): Confucian classics
Zhongyong.note: Component chapter of Liji; Hanshu 30 also has Zhongyong shuo under Six Arts > Rites. Cited page confirms it was originally a chapter in the Classic of Rites.

Zhuangzi.label: Masters: Daoist (Daojia)
Zhuangzi.note: Hanshu 30 lists Zhuangzi, 52 pian, under Daojia; cited page identifies it as foundational Daoist.

region.title: Regional-origin taxonomy of early Chinese thought texts (six regions)
region.source_claim: Proposed by the Six Schools Lab Advocate on 2026-10-03 as an experimental rival to Sima Tan's inherited six-schools taxonomy: instead of 'school', each transmitted book is labelled by the regional culture of its traditionally attributed author or principal place of compilation, following Shiji-rooted attributions and modern regional-culture scholarship (Qi/Jixia academy studies, Chu-southern Daodejia culture, Qin Legalism, Lu-Zou Confucian-Mohian milieu, Central Plains Jin-successor states, and Wu-Yue military tradition). Attribution rule: assign the region of the traditionally attributed author's origin or service; when the attributed author is legendary or disputed, assign the region of the dominant place-of-compilation account and mark 'contested'.

Analects.label: Lu-Zou (Lu Confucian-Mohian ritual milieu)
Analects.note: Compiled by followers of Confucius, who taught in Lu; the corpus's Lu provenance is the standard scholarly account.

Gongsun_Longzi.label: Central Plains (Jin successor states and Song)
Gongsun_Longzi.note: Gongsun Long was traditionally a man of Zhao and retainer of Lord Pingyuan; one alternative note (Gao You) calls him a Wei man.

Guanzi.label: Qi-Jixia (Jixia academy and Qi statecraft)
Guanzi.note: Named for the Qi minister Guan Zhong but anonymous; much of the material is associated with the 4th-c. BCE Jixia Academy in Linzi.

Guiguzi.label: Central Plains (Jin successor states and Song)
Guiguzi.note: Origin theories divide between Wey and Wei (Central Plains) with other legendary locations; no secure attribution.

Han_Feizi.label: Central Plains (Jin successor states and Song)
Han_Feizi.note: Han Fei was a clansman of the state of Han; the anthology is traditionally attributed to him.

Huainanzi.label: Chu-South (Chu and southern Daodejia culture)
Huainanzi.note: Product of Liu An's Huainan (Chu region) court; translators also describe it as maintaining and extending the Jixia (Qi) tradition, so Chu placement is flagged.

Huangdi_Sijing.note: Sealed excavated manuscript; intentionally not labelled.

Kongzi_Jiayu.label: Lu-Zou (Lu Confucian-Mohian ritual milieu)
Kongzi_Jiayu.note: Confucius lore and disciple records (Lu tradition), but the received text's compilation was long disputed and associated with Wang Su (Cao Wei); excavated copies have only partially rehabilitated it.

Laozi.label: Chu-South (Chu and southern Daodejia culture)
Laozi.note: Traditional accounts place Laozi in the 6th-c. BCE state of Chu, but his historicity and the text's authorship are heavily debated.

Liezi.label: Central Plains (Jin successor states and Song)
Liezi.note: Lie Yukou is traditionally a man of Zheng (Central Plains), but the received text may be a much later (c. 4th c. CE) compilation.

Liji.label: Lu-Zou (Lu Confucian-Mohian ritual milieu)
Liji.note: A diverse Confucian ritual compilation of uncertain origin; its pre-Han/Han ritual-transmission milieu is the Lu-Zou Confucian tradition.

Liutao.label: Qi-Jixia (Jixia academy and Qi statecraft)
Liutao.note: Traditionally attributed to Jiang Ziya (Taigong), later enfeoffed at Qi; some scholars see vestiges of ancient Qi military thought, but composition is Warring States and attribution legendary.

Lushi_Chunqiu.label: Qin (Qin Legalist and late pre-imperial compilation)
Lushi_Chunqiu.note: Compiled c. 239 BCE under Qin chancellor Lü Buwei and almost certainly written for Qin authorities.

Mencius.label: Lu-Zou (Lu Confucian-Mohian ritual milieu)
Mencius.note: Mencius was born in the state of Zou (Zoucheng, Shandong); he later taught at Jixia but the attributed author is Zou/Lu-region.

Mozi.label: Lu-Zou (Lu Confucian-Mohian ritual milieu)
Mozi.note: Most sources describe Mozi as from Lu, though one says Song; Lu is followed here with the disagreement flagged.

Shangjunshu.label: Qin (Qin Legalist and late pre-imperial compilation)
Shangjunshu.note: Attributed to Shang Yang, the major Qin reformer under Duke Xiao; chapters include Qin court discourses, though some material is later.

Sima_Fa.label: Qi-Jixia (Jixia academy and Qi statecraft)
Sima_Fa.note: The text is described as developed in the state of Qi during the 4th century BCE.

Sun_Bin_Bingfa.note: Sealed excavated manuscript; intentionally not labelled.

Sunzi_Bingfa.label: Wu-Yue (southeastern military tradition)
Sunzi_Bingfa.note: Shiji tradition: Sun Wu was from Qi and served the king of Wu; the Wu-service attribution is used, with Qi origin noted as competing.

Wei_Liaozi.label: Qin (Qin Legalist and late pre-imperial compilation)
Wei_Liaozi.note: The Shiji casts Wei Liao as advisor to the young king of Qin (Shi Huang), but authorship is poorly evidenced and two same-titled works existed in Han.

Wuzi.label: Central Plains (Jin successor states and Song)
Wuzi.note: Wu Qi was born in the state of Wei (魏), though he later served Lu, Wei/West River, and finally Chu.

Xiaojing.label: Lu-Zou (Lu Confucian-Mohian ritual milieu)
Xiaojing.note: Presented as a Confucius-Zengzi dialogue; author unknown, but framed within the Lu Confucian school.

Xunzi.label: Qi-Jixia (Jixia academy and Qi statecraft)
Xunzi.note: Xun Zi is listed among the renowned Confucian philosophers of the Jixia Academy in Linzi, the Qi capital.

Zhongyong.label: Lu-Zou (Lu Confucian-Mohian ritual milieu)
Zhongyong.note: Traditionally attributed to Zisi, grandson of Confucius (Lu); modern scholars debate date and authorship.

Zhuangzi.label: Chu-South (Chu and southern Daodejia culture)
Zhuangzi.note: Most historians place Zhuang Zhou's birth at Meng in Song, while the Shiji tradition links him with Chu (and Linzi); the southern-Chu Daoist attribution is used but contested.

six.title: Sima Tan six-schools taxonomy (Shiji 130, 'Lun liujia yaozhi')
six.source_claim: Formalization of the six-school scheme of Sima Tan (d. 110 BCE), 'Lun liujia yaozhi' / 'Essential Meanings of the Six Schools', Shiji ch. 130 (reprinted in Taishigong zixu): Yinyangjia, Rujia, Mojia, Mingjia, Fajia, Daojia (Daodejia). Book-level assignments follow the earliest extant bibliographic tradition, Hanshu ch. 30 'Yiwenzhi' (Ban Gu, 1st c. CE), cross-checked against modern reference scholarship: M. Loewe (ed.), Early Chinese Texts: A Bibliographical Guide (Berkeley: Society for the Study of Early China, 1993); K. Smith Jr., 'Sima Tan and the Invention of Daoism: Legist Thought and the Han', Journal of Asian Studies 62.1 (2003): 129-156. CODEBOOK: (1) Sima Tan's scheme has no Bingjia (military) or Zajia (syncretist) slot, though the Hanshu Yiwenzhi uses both; every such transmitted book receives a documented forced-choice nearest-school assignment and is marked 'contested'. (2) Confucian classics (Li, Xiao Jing, Zhongyong) stand under the Yiwenzhi jing-divisions rather than the zi 'Rujia' shelf; the codebook maps the Ru classics/tradition to Confucian. (3) Where catalog assignment changed over time (Guanzi: Daojia in Yiwenzhi, Fajia from Sui shu Jingji zhi on), the earliest attested Han assignment is used and the unit marked 'contested'. (4) Sealed excavated units (Huangdi_Sijing, Sun_Bin_Bingfa) are never labelled; they are the held-out tomb test.

Analects.label: Confucian
Analects.note: Yiwenzhi lists Lunyu under the jing-division 'Lunyu' class; core of Sima Tan's Rujia tradition (Shiji 130: Rujia 'you xu xue, bei song shuo'). Codebook rule 2.

Gongsun_Longzi.label: School of Names
Gongsun_Longzi.note: Yiwenzhi Mingjia: Gongsun Longzi shisi pian. Only substantially transmitted Mingjia text; uncontested (surviving 6 pian authenticity debated, class not).

Guanzi.label: Daoist
Guanzi.note: CODEBOOK DECISION (the textbook case): Hanshu Yiwenzhi lists Guanzi ba shiliu pian under Daojia; from the Sui shu Jingji zhi (636 CE) onward it is re-catalogued under Fajia, and much modern scholarship (e.g. Rickett) reads it as a Qi/Jixia legalist-statecraft compilation with Daoist (Xinshu, Neiye, Baixin) chapters. Codebook rule 3: follow the earliest attested Han assignment (Daojia) since the taxonomy being audited is Han-dynastic (Sima Tan / Ban Gu). Contested.

Guiguzi.label: School of Names
Guiguzi.note: CODEBOOK DECISION: traditionally founder-text of the Zonghengjia (School of Diplomacy), which Sima Tan's six do not include; later absorbed into the Daoist canon. Forced choice per rule 1: School of Names, on its program of bian (disputation), rhetoric and shi/persuasion theory, the closest six-school analogue to the diplomats' arts. Rival candidate: Daoist (canon absorption). Contested.

Han_Feizi.label: Legalist
Han_Feizi.note: CODEBOOK DECISION: labelled Legalist, the canonical assignment (Shiji 63; Yiwenzhi Fajia: Hanzi wushiwu pian; A.C. Graham's 'great synthesizer' of Legalism). Marked contested because chs. 20-21 (Jie Lao / Yu Lao) are Laozi commentaries generally treated as Huang-Lao/Daoist addenda, and Sima Qian roots Han Fei's learning in Huang-Lao before turning to xingming fashu. Unit-level label follows the dominant tradition (codebook rule 1).

Huainanzi.label: Daoist
Huainanzi.note: Yiwenzhi Daojia: Huainan nei ershiyi pian (outer chapters lost). Standard class: Daoist (Huang-Lao court syncretism under Liu An). Medium rather than high because its dense yin-yang/correlative cosmology (Tianwen xun) makes it the strongest Yin-Yang claimant in the transmitted corpus; codebook keeps the attested Han catalog assignment.

Huangdi_Sijing.note: SEALED excavated unit (Mawangdui silk manuscripts, buried 168 BCE). Held-out tomb test: deliberately NOT labelled per lab protocol. (The received tradition would later attach such Huang-Lao texts to Daojia; that inference is the experiment, not the codebook.)

Kongzi_Jiayu.label: Confucian
Kongzi_Jiayu.note: Yiwenzhi Rujia: Kongzi Jiayu ershiqi pian. Once dismissed as a Wang Su (3rd c. CE) forgery; partly rehabilitated by excavated parallels (Loewe ed. 1993). Class assignment itself uncontested; only date/authenticity disputed.

Laozi.label: Daoist
Laozi.note: Anchor text of Sima Tan's Daojia (= Daodejia; Shiji 130 praises Laozi/Zhuangzi by name). Han bibliographic placement nuanced (Yiwenzhi Daojia lists Laozi commentaries); class uncontested.

Liezi.label: Daoist
Liezi.note: Yiwenzhi Daojia: Liezi ba pian. Received text likely a Wei-Jin (3rd-4th c. CE) recompilation, but the catalog class assignment is Daoist in every dynastic bibliography; the date dispute does not make the class contested.

Liji.label: Confucian
Liji.note: Yiwenzhi jing-division 'Li' class (Ji by 130 pian), not the zi-level Rujia shelf; mapped to Confucian per codebook rule 2. Contains 'Yueling' correlative material, but the transmitted book is canonically Ru.

Liutao.label: Daoist
Liutao.note: CODEBOOK DECISION: Yiwenzhi Bingjia: Tai Gong ershibai san shisi pian; received Liutao attributed to Lu Shang (Jiang Taigong) and datable no earlier than Warring States. Bingjia absent from the six; forced choice Daoist, following the Qi/Huang-Lao statecraft tradition and the text's later absorption into Tai Gong/Daoist lore. Rival candidate: Confucian (its benevolent-government 'Civil Strategy' rhetoric). Contested.

Lushi_Chunqiu.label: Yin-Yang
Lushi_Chunqiu.note: CODEBOOK DECISION: Yiwenzhi classifies it Zajia (syncretist) - a seventh shelf with no counterpart in Sima Tan's six (and, as the tradition notes, 'no school called itself Syncretist'). Forced into the six, assigned to Yin-Yang on the strength of its Twelve Ji framework, a month-by-month yin-yang/wuxing correlative almanac in the Zou Yan tradition (Yiwenzhi Yinyangjia anchor figure; cf. Yueling-type material). Rival candidates: Daoist (Huang-Lao statecraft) or Confucian (Ru anecdotal density). Contested; illustrates the six-school scheme's failure to accommodate imperial syncretism.

Mencius.label: Confucian
Mencius.note: Yiwenzhi Rujia: Mengzi shiyi pian. Uncontested in Hanshu and modern scholarship (Loewe ed. 1993).

Mozi.label: Mohist
Mozi.note: Yiwenzhi Mojia: Mozi qi shiyi pian. The single transmitted Mohist text; uncontested.

Shangjunshu.label: Legalist
Shangjunshu.note: Yiwenzhi Fajia: Shangjun shu ershi'jiu pian. Standard Legalist assignment; composite Warring States text but class uncontested.

Sima_Fa.label: Confucian
Sima_Fa.note: CODEBOOK DECISION: Yiwenzhi Bingjia: Junli Sima Fa yi bai wushiwu pian; developed in 4th-c. Qi. Bingjia absent from the six; forced choice Confucian - by the Eastern Han Ban Gu already treated it as a rites (li) work, and the text's wen/wu ritual complementarity and just-war morality are the most Ru-inflected of the military classics. Rival candidate: Legalist (its fa/regulation content). Contested.

Sun_Bin_Bingfa.note: SEALED excavated unit (Yinqueshan bamboo slips, tomb closed c. 134 BCE). Held-out tomb test: deliberately NOT labelled per lab protocol.

Sunzi_Bingfa.label: Daoist
Sunzi_Bingfa.note: CODEBOOK DECISION: Yiwenzhi classifies it Bingjia (quanmou) - military shelf absent from Sima Tan's six. Forced choice: Daoist, on the text's own dao/xu/shi/xing-formless idiom and the well-attested scholarly linkage of Sunzi's 'inaction and impartiality' philosophy to Daoist thought (cf. Han Feizi article; Mair/Ames readings; the Yinque shan 'Sunzi' commentary tradition). Alternative reading treats it as class-external to the six - itself evidence for the audit. Contested.

Wei_Liaozi.label: Legalist
Wei_Liaozi.note: CODEBOOK DECISION: Yiwenzhi Bingjia: Wei Liao ershi'jiu pian (a Wei Liaozi also appears under Zajia in some catalog traditions); text set at the Qin court, where Li Si praised Wei Liao. Bingjia absent from the six; forced choice Legalist on its agriculture-war, rewards-and-punishments statecraft, the standard modern characterization as a 'legalist military text'. Rival candidate: treat as Bingjia class-external. Contested.

Wuzi.label: Confucian
Wuzi.note: CODEBOOK DECISION: Seven Military Classic (Bingjia shelf, absent from the six). Forced choice: Confucian - the received text is a dialogue of Wu Qi (traditionally a Zeng Shen-lineage Ru student) with Marquis Wu of Wei whose philosophy is explicitly 'a synthesis between Confucianism and Legalism' weighted to benevolent government and moral values. Rival candidate: Legalist (rewards-and-punishments half of the synthesis). Contested.

Xiaojing.label: Confucian
Xiaojing.note: Yiwenzhi jing-division 'Xiaojing' class; codebook rule 2 maps the Ru classics tradition to Confucian.

Xunzi.label: Confucian
Xunzi.note: Yiwenzhi Rujia: Sun Qing shu sanshi'er pian (Xunzi). Standard assignment; note his two Legalist students (Han Fei, Li Si) do not change the book's class.

Zhongyong.label: Confucian
Zhongyong.note: Chapter of Liji; Yiwenzhi also lists a separate Zhongyong er pian under Rujia. Confucian assignment uncontested.

Zhuangzi.label: Daoist
Zhuangzi.note: Yiwenzhi Daojia: Zhuangzi wushi'er pian. Named in Shiji 130 alongside Laozi as Daojia exemplar.

payload.objective: Audit inherited taxonomies of thought: is a taxonomy a structure already present in the texts (discovered) or a label imposed later (invented)? Use two leak-free designs: a sealed text (Mawangdui manuscript, buried 168 BCE) and a sealed reader (a language model trained only on pre-1931 text).

H-C1.claim: The six-schools taxonomy predicts where an unseen book falls better than era, region or genre taxonomies.
H-C1.decision: rank by chance-corrected score with 95% bootstrap interval; require agreement across instruments (lex, lex_tr) for a main claim

H-C2.claim: The instrument ranks chapters that scholars regard as Daoist-leaning (Guanzi: Neiye, Xinshu I-II, Baixin; Han Feizi: Jie Lao, Yu Lao) high on Daoist affinity within their own books.
H-C2.decision: PASS if mean target percentile >= 80 and permutation p < 0.05; otherwise the instrument fails validation and no main conclusion may be published

H-C3.claim: The sealed manuscript sits between Dao and Fa instead of falling cleanly into one school.
H-C3.decision: 'constructed' prediction holds if dominant label share < 0.70 OR mean margin below the 10th percentile of transmitted books; otherwise the 'real structure' prediction holds

H-W1.claim: A reader sealed in 1930 already separates what was later called analytic vs continental philosophy.

H-W2.claim: A modern reader separates the later label more sharply than the 1930 reader, beyond its general advantage on labels that already existed in 1930 (hindsight gap G > 0).

decision_rules_after_first_tournament: If the six-schools taxonomy leads AND the tomb test supports 'real structure': next experiment = extend the sealed-text test to the Guodian slips.

If the six-schools taxonomy leads BUT the tomb test supports 'constructed': rewrite the conclusion as 'school structure holds in Han-edited transmitted books but not out of sample'; prioritise the translation-arm rerun.
If an era, region or genre taxonomy leads: reopen the premise that the school is the basic unit; next experiment = school test within era strata.

A pipeline smoke test with a throwaway labelling was run during tool development; it is not a reported result. All taxonomies, experiment choices, runs, critiques and conclusions below are produced by the Omnigent agents.

payload.title: Sima Tan's six schools (Lun liujia yaozhi, Shiji 130): Yin-Yang, Confucian, Mohist, Names, Legalist, Daoist
payload.source_claim: Six-fold partition of the early Chinese masters proposed by Sima Tan (Grand Astrologer, d. 110 BCE) in his essay 'Lun liujia yaozhi' (論六家要旨), preserved in Shiji ch. 130 (Taishigong zixu), completed by his son Sima Qian ca. 91 BCE; Tan's essay names yinyang jia, ru jia, mo jia, ming jia, fa jia and dao jia (documented at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sima_Tan and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Schools_of_Thought). This taxonomy transfers Tan's six labels onto the 23 transmitted books of the corpus, following the Han bibliographic tradition (Hanshu Yiwenzhi; context in Hunter 2019, https://doi.org/10.7817/jameroriesoci.138.4.0763) and standard sinological reference works. Books that Han bibliography placed in categories OUTSIDE the six schools (military/bing, ritual canon, Zajia eclectics, Zongheng diplomacy) are force-assigned to the least-bad class and marked contested; the Yin-Yang class receives no book because its central figure Zou Yan's writings are all lost (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zou_Yan).

payload.claim: T_six formalizes Sima Tan's six-school partition (Lun liujia yaozhi, Shiji 130, ca. 100 BCE; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sima_Tan) over the 23 transmitted books. Partition: Confucian 8 (Analects, Mencius, Xunzi, Liji*, Xiaojing, Kongzi_Jiayu, Zhongyong, Sima_Fa*), Daoist 9 (Laozi, Zhuangzi, Liezi*, Guanzi*, Lushi_Chunqiu*, Huainanzi*, Guiguzi*, Sunzi_Bingfa*, Liutao*), Legalist 4 (Han_Feizi, Shangjunshu, Wuzi*, Wei_Liaozi*), Mohist 1 (Mozi), Names 1 (Gongsun_Longzi), Yin-Yang 0. * = contested (11 units total).
key_findings: Yin-Yang class is necessarily EMPTY: its central figure Zou Yan's writings are all lost (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zou_Yan); no transmitted book in this corpus is a yin-yang school text. The six-schools partition cannot fill one of its own classes from the transmitted corpus.

Five books (Sunzi_Bingfa, Wuzi, Liutao, Sima_Fa, Wei_Liaozi) are Seven Military Classics texts that Han bibliography filed in the bing (military) category, outside the six schools; all are contested force-assignments.
Guanzi: Hanshu Yiwenzhi = Daoist, Suishu = Legalist, modern = syncretic Jixia composite (https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/管子_(書)); assigned Daoist per the earliest Han classification.

Lushi_Chunqiu and Huainanzi were both Zajia (Syncretist) in Han bibliography; both assigned Daoist (Huang-Lao reading) per modern scholarship (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huainanzi; https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/呂氏春秋), noting the Siku quanshu read Lushi_Chunqiu as Confucian-dominant.
Sima Fa was classified by Ban Gu as a work of rites/li (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Methods_of_the_Sima), supporting its contested Confucian assignment.

Liutao is the ONLY unit with citation 'uncertain': its Taigong corpus is traditionally placed in the Yiwenzhi Daoist category, but no citable URL was retrievable from the lab tools; assignment documented as least-bad, not source-backed.
disputed: Lushi_Chunqiu (Zajia; Huang-Lao Daoist vs Siku Confucian reading)
Liezi (received text ca. 4th c. CE compilation vs Han text)
Guiguzi (Zongheng school text later in Daoist canon)
Sunzi_Bingfa, Wuzi, Liutao, Sima_Fa, Wei_Liaozi (military-category texts with no natural six-school class)
Liji (ritual canon vs ru jia masters category)

payload.title: Liu Xin / Ban Gu nine-streams scheme (Hanshu Yiwenzhi, early 1st c. CE)
payload.source_claim: Proposed by Liu Xin (Qilue, c. late 1st c. BCE - 23 CE) and preserved by Ban Gu in the Yiwenzhi bibliographic treatise (Hanshu ch. 30, by 111 CE), which organizes all known literature into six divisions and whose 'Zhuzi lüe' defines the ten schools / nine streams (jiuliu shijia). Documented at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yiwenzhi and https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/藝文志 ('九流十家'一詞便出自《漢書藝文志略序》); studied in Hunter 2019, JAOS, https://doi.org/10.7817/jameroriesoci.138.4.0763. Each book is placed in the Yiwenzhi category where the catalog records it; least-best-fit assignments marked contested. Sealed excavated units (Huangdi_Sijing, Sun_Bin_Bingfa) are excluded entirely and receive no label.

payload.claim: Taxonomy T_yiwenzhi_nine (sha256 d825b4f91c9429503669274dc329d7aa24944077dfbab5961ff810710fff035c) formalizes the Liu Xin / Ban Gu nine-streams scheme from the Hanshu Yiwenzhi (Hanshu ch. 30, early 1st c. CE) over the 23 transmitted zh books; 9 classes, n=23, n_contested=5 (Kongzi_Jiayu, Liezi, Guiguzi, Liutao, Wei_Liaozi); 1 uncertain citation (Liutao). Sealed units Huangdi_Sijing and Sun_Bin_Bingfa unlabelled.
disputed_or_notable: Guanzi is placed under Daoists because the Yiwenzhi itself lists it in Daojia; the Fajia placement is Sui-period (zh Wikipedia explicit). This diverges from modern and six-school intuitions and is a key discriminator vs rival taxonomies.
Sima_Fa is placed under Six Arts (Ritual) as junli Sima Fa, per Ban Gu's own classification (en Wikipedia explicit); its later bingjia status is post-Han.

Liutao is placed under Daoists via the Yiwenzhi's parent Taigong 237 pian entry (incl. bing 85 pian) registered in Daojia; citation marked 'uncertain' because no tool-verified URL stated this placement explicitly.
Guiguzi is absent from the Yiwenzhi; Strategists (Zonghengjia) assignment is a least-best fit via Sui catalog tradition.
Wei_Liaozi has dual Yiwenzhi entries (Zajia 31 pian vs Military 29 pian); Military chosen per majority/Yinqueshan identification, marked contested.
Kongzi Jiayu IS recorded in the Yiwenzhi (27 juan) within the Confucian tradition, but the received Wang Su text's relation to that entry is disputed.
Liezi recorded in Yiwenzhi Daojia (8 pian) but received text likely 4th-c. CE compilation; contested.

payload.claim: Sima Tan (c. 165-110 BCE), Grand Astrologer under Emperor Wu of Han, is the traditional author of the essay 'Lun liujia yaozhi' (Essential Meanings of the Six Schools), preserved as part of Shiji ch. 130 (Taishigong zixu), the autobiographical postface of Sima Qian's Shiji (composed late 2nd-early 1st c. BCE, building on Sima Tan's drafts; Tan died 110 BCE). The essay evaluates six kinds of governance/scholarly traditions using 'jia' (family/expert) labels: Yinyangjia (Naturalists, central figure Zou Yan), Rujia (Confucians), Mojia (Mohists), Mingjia (School of Names), Fajia (Legalists), and Daojia (Dao school). Per Kidder Smith (2003), Daojia — and likewise 'Legalism' (Fajia) — are Sima Tan's retrospective coinages: the essay invents these categories to group heterogeneous thinkers, and is primarily an argument FOR the Daojia (a wuwei-centered, Huang-Lao-inflected statecraft) against the shortcomings of the other five.
contested: Date of composition: no independent attestation. Standard accounts place it late in Tan's life (he died 110 BCE, the year of the fengshan sacrifice from which he was excluded — the Shiji frames the essay near his death); Kidder Smith treats it as an early-Wu-reign text and his 2003 article is the standard re-examination of its date, authorship and intent. Preregistered dating for our purposes: between 141 BCE (Wu accession) and 110 BCE (Tan's death).

Whether the jia categories were 'invented' by Tan or reported existing discourse: Smith (2003) argues invention (esp. Daojia/Fajia/Mingjia as new labels); the Huang-Lao wiki synthesis notes Tan likely coined Daojia with existing Huang-Lao literature in mind; Lee (2014) shows 'Ru-Mo' pairings in pre-imperial texts may not map onto the received 'Confucian/Mohist schools' reading — i.e., at least Ru and Mo have some pre-imperial attestation as designations, while the sixfold scheme as a system is Han.

Whether Tan's 'jia' meant 'school' at all: Wikipedia's Sima Tan article stresses 'jia' could mean 'expert' or 'family'; it likely did not occur to Tan that the categories would be used as historical schools with memberships.
sources: https://doi.org/10.2307/3096138 (Kidder Smith, 'Sima Tan and the Invention of Daoism, "Legalism," et cetera', Journal of Asian Studies 62.1 (2003): 129-156; DOI verified — resolves to JAS 62/1/129)
https://doi.org/10.13173/oe.53.1.111 (Ting-mien Lee, 'When Ru-Mo May Not Be Confucians and Mohists', Oriens Extremus 53 (2014); URL verified)
