T_1930.title: The circa-1930 English-language school partition: absolute idealism vs Kantian critical philosophy vs pragmatism vs realism (new/critical) vs philosophy-of-life/voluntarism vs positivism-utilitarian empiricism
T_1930.source_claim: The partition a well-read English-language reader of c.1930 would have used, documented entirely in pre-1931 sources: R. B. Perry, The Present Conflict of Ideals (1918) maps the standing camps (idealism, pragmatism, realism); Holt/Marvin/Montague/Perry/Pitkin/Spaulding, 'The Program and First Platform of Six Realists' (J. Phil. 7, 1910) and The New Realism (1912) name 'the new realism' and claim Moore and Russell as its anti-idealist forerunners; Essays in Critical Realism (1920, contributions by Santayana, Strong, Lovejoy, Sellars, Drake, Pratt, Rogers) names 'critical realism'; W. James, Pragmatism (1907) names pragmatism and lists Dewey's 'Chicago school'; C. S. Peirce, 'What Pragmatism Is' and 'The Issues of Pragmaticism' (Monist, 1905) name pragmatism/pragmaticism; H. Hoeffding, History of Modern Philosophy (Eng. trans. 1900) and F. Bowen, Modern Philosophy from Descartes to Schopenhauer and Hartmann (1877/1879) supply 'voluntarism/pessimism' as the standing rubric for Schopenhauer and his heirs; R. Eucken, Main Currents of Modern Thought (Eng. trans. 1912) and Knowledge and Life (Eng. 1913) document the life-philosophy/activism current; J. S. Mill, Auguste Comte and Positivism (1865; 5th ed. 1907) names 'positivism'; J. Seth, 'The Ethical System of Henry Sidgwick' (Mind, 1901) and Sidgwick, 'The Philosophy of T. H. Green' (Mind, 1901) document the utilitarian-vs-idealist sorting of the Cambridge moralists. The analytic/continental vocabulary is deliberately absent: it did not exist as a classification before 1931.

Bergson.label: Philosophy of life / voluntarism (irrationalist reaction)
Bergson.note: J. E. Russell, 'Bergson's Anti-Intellectualism' (J. Phil. Psych. Sci. Meth. 9, 1912): the standard pre-1931 English sorting of Bergson as intuitionist/vitalist philosopher of life; Creative Evolution Eng. trans. 1911 (doi:10.5962/bhl.title.166289).

Bosanquet.label: Absolute idealism (Hegelian/neo-Hegelian)
Bosanquet.note: S. W. Dyde's review of The Philosophical Theory of the State (Philosophical Review 9, 1900) places Bosanquet with Green in British Hegelian idealism.

Comte.label: Positivism and utilitarian empiricism
Comte.note: Mill, Auguste Comte and Positivism (1865; 5th ed. 1907): Comte is the name-giver of positivism; A General View of Positivism (Eng. trans. Bridges, 1865) was his own English-facing statement.

Croce.label: Absolute idealism (Hegelian/neo-Hegelian)
Croce.note: G. W. Cunningham's review of Croce, What is Living and What is Dead of the Philosophy of Hegel (Eng. trans. Ainslie; Philosophical Review 25, 1916): Croce received in English as a neo-Hegelian 'philosophy of spirit' idealist.

Dewey.label: Pragmatism (pragmaticism/instrumentalism)
Dewey.note: James's Pragmatism (1907) names Dewey's 'Chicago school' of pragmatism; Lovejoy's review of Perry, The Present Conflict of Ideals (Harvard Theological Review, 1920) documents pragmatism, incl. Dewey's 'instrumentalism', as one of the standing camps.

Eucken.label: Philosophy of life / voluntarism (irrationalist reaction)
Eucken.note: Contested: Eucken's 'activism'/independent spiritual life-philosophy (Knowledge and Life, Eng. 1913; Main Currents of Modern Thought, Eng. trans. 1912; W. T. Jones, An Interpretation of Rudolf Eucken's Philosophy, 1912) was sorted by some pre-1931 surveys as a new idealism and by others alongside Bergson as life-philosophy; placed with the life-philosophy current.

Green.label: Absolute idealism (Hegelian/neo-Hegelian)
Green.note: Sidgwick, 'The Philosophy of T. H. Green' (Mind 10, 1901): Green canonically sorted as founder of the British neo-Hegelian/idealist revival; his Prolegomena to Ethics (1883) argues against empiricism from idealist premises.

Hegel.label: Absolute idealism (Hegelian/neo-Hegelian)
Hegel.note: J. E. Creighton's review of W. Wallace, The Logic of Hegel, 2nd ed. (Philosophical Review 4, 1895) treats Hegel as the head of absolute idealism; Wallace's Prolegomena (1874/1892) was the standard English presentation.

James.label: Pragmatism (pragmaticism/instrumentalism)
James.note: James, Pragmatism: A New Name for Some Old Ways of Thinking (1907) - the school's name-giving manifesto (contemporary review: Phil. Rev. 16, 1907, doi:10.2307/2177297).

Kant.label: Critical philosophy (Kantian transcendental idealism)
Kant.note: E. Caird, 'Kant's Refutation of Idealism' (Mind os-5, 1880, and companion piece by Sidgwick, doi:10.1093/mind/os-v.17.111): c.1900 English scholarship sorts Kant as 'transcendental/critical idealist' distinct from Hegelian absolute idealism; the neo-Kantian label for his successors was current by 1930.

Kierkegaard.label: Philosophy of life / voluntarism (irrationalist reaction)
Kierkegaard.note: Contested: barely a school figure for 1930 English readers; pre-1931 sources (Hoeffding, Soeren Kierkegaard als Philosoph, 1896, Germ. ed. 1910 - documented at the cited URL; Brandes, Main Currents, Eng. trans. 1901-05) sort him as religious anti-Hegelian philosopher of subjective existence/will rather than under any recognized '-ism'.

Mach.label: Positivism and utilitarian empiricism
Mach.note: Contested: Washburn's review of Contributions to the Analysis of the Sensations (Eng. trans. 1897; Philosophical Review 6, 1897, and E. A. Singer in Science 6, 1897, doi:10.1126/science.6.152.810.b) shows pre-1931 sources alternating among 'positivist', 'empirio-criticist' (with Avenarius) and 'phenomenalist' for Mach; sorted here in the positivist current.

Mill.label: Positivism and utilitarian empiricism
Mill.note: Sorted pre-1931 in the empiricist-utilitarian-positivist line (System of Logic 1843; Utilitarianism 1863; Auguste Comte and Positivism 1865) even though Mill also criticized Comte's later 'religion of humanity'.

Moore.label: Realism (new realism/critical realism)
Moore.note: Moore, 'The Refutation of Idealism' (Mind 12, 1903) was cited by the six new realists as the opening move of the realist revolt (Holt et al., 'The Program and First Platform of Six Realists', J. Phil. 7, 1910, doi:10.2307/2010710).

Nietzsche.label: Philosophy of life / voluntarism (irrationalist reaction)
Nietzsche.note: Contested: W. M. Salter's review (Harvard Theological Review 8, 1915) of Carus, Nietzsche and Other Exponents of Individualism (1914), Mencken, The Philosophy of Friedrich Nietzsche (1908/1913) and Chatterton-Hill (1914) shows pre-1931 English sources variously sorting him as individualist, Schopenhauerian voluntarist, or aristocratic irrationalist - grouped here as Schopenhauer's voluntarist heir.

Peirce.label: Pragmatism (pragmaticism/instrumentalism)
Peirce.note: Contested: Peirce founded pragmatism ('What Pragmatism Is', Monist 15, 1905, doi:10.5840/monist190515230) but in 'The Issues of Pragmaticism' (Monist 15, 1905) he renames his doctrine 'pragmaticism' and repudiates the James-Dewey version - pre-1931 sources disagree on whether he belongs to the school he named.

Perry.label: Realism (new realism/critical realism)
Perry.note: Perry was one of the signatories of 'The Program and First Platform of Six Realists' (J. Phil. 7, 1910) and a co-author of The New Realism (1912); his Present Conflict of Ideals (1918) speaks for the realist camp.

Poincare.label: Positivism and utilitarian empiricism
Poincare.note: Contested: The Foundations of Science (Eng. trans. Halsted, Putnam 1913, intro. Josiah Royce - the pre-1931 edition behind the cited DOI): English readers sorted Poincare with Mach as scientist-positivist/conventionalist, while others called his conventionalism a critical-rationalist departure from positivism.

Royce.label: Absolute idealism (Hegelian/neo-Hegelian)
Royce.note: Creighton's review of Royce's posthumous Lectures on Modern Idealism (Philosophical Review 30, 1921); Dewey's reviews of The World and the Individual (Phil. Rev. 9, 1900, doi:10.2307/2176386) already sorted Royce as the American absolutist.

Russell.label: Realism (new realism/critical realism)
Russell.note: Contested: Lovejoy's review of The New Realism (Science 37, 1913) reflects how the 1912 realists claimed Russell (and Moore) as leaders of the anti-idealist revolt, yet de Laguna's review of The Problems of Philosophy (Phil. Rev. 22, 1913, doi:10.2307/2178182) already treats Russell as an independent Cambridge logician-analyst rather than a school realist; Russell himself refused the label.

Santayana.label: Realism (new realism/critical realism)
Santayana.note: Santayana contributed to Essays in Critical Realism (1920) with Drake, Lovejoy, Pratt, Rogers, Sellars and Strong; Perry's review (Phil. Rev. 30, 1921) lists him under critical realism.

Schopenhauer.label: Philosophy of life / voluntarism (irrationalist reaction)
Schopenhauer.note: F. Bowen, Modern Philosophy from Descartes to Schopenhauer and Hartmann (ch. 'Arthur Schopenhauer: Pessimism, aesthetics, ethics'): sorted pre-1931 as the voluntarist/pessimist who makes will, not intellect, primary; Hoeffding (Eng. 1900) heads his voluntarism section with Schopenhauer.

Sidgwick.label: Positivism and utilitarian empiricism
Sidgwick.note: Contested: J. Seth, 'The Ethical System of Henry Sidgwick' (Mind 10, 1901) sorts him as the era's philosophical utilitarian, yet pre-1931 obituaries/tributes (L. Stephen, Mind 10, 1901, doi:10.1093/mind/x.1.1) also group him with the Cambridge idealist milieu of Green and McTaggart - placed with utilitarian empiricism.

Spencer.label: Positivism and utilitarian empiricism
Spencer.note: B. P. Bowne, The Philosophy of Herbert Spencer (examining First Principles): Spencer grouped with Comte/Mill as scientific-empiricist positivist by pre-1931 historians, though also styled 'the synthetic/evolutionary philosopher' and an agnostic - hence medium rather than high.

Whitehead.label: Realism (new realism/critical realism)
Whitehead.note: Contested: L. S. Stebbing's review of Science and the Modern World (Philosophy 1, 1926) shows 1920s readers splitting over whether Whitehead's 'philosophy of organism' is a realism of nature (as The Concept of Nature suggested) or a speculative idealism-leaning cosmology; placed with realism on the strength of his early nature-philosophy reception.

T_era.title: Era / stratigraphic partition of early Chinese masters literature (composition/final-compilation dating)
T_era.source_claim: No single ancient proponent: this is the modern 'era' comparator pre-registered in the lab's hypothesis H-C1 (six-schools taxonomy vs era/region/genre), built from modern transmitted-text dating scholarship (the Loewe 'Early Chinese Texts' tradition; Brooks & Brooks accretional model; Guodian-informed Laozi dating; Pines on the Book of Lord Shang; Sato on the Guanzi; Graham-school view of the Liezi). Class set: 5 composition strata from Spring-and-Autumn/early Warring States to post-Han compilation. Each book is assigned by its period of composition/final compilation per the cited literature; where dating is disputed the majority/least-bad reading is taken and confidence is marked 'contested'.

Analects.label: Middle Warring States (c. 400-300 BCE)
Analects.note: Consensus: large portions composed during the Warring States period; final form mid-Han. Layered composition (Brooks & Brooks accretion 479-249 BCE); assigned to mid-WS by dominant composition stratum.

Gongsun_Longzi.label: Late Warring States (c. 300-221 BCE)
Gongsun_Longzi.note: Essays associated with Gongsun Long (c. 320-250 BCE); 6 of 14 original essays extant, some possibly later.

Guanzi.label: Qin-Western Han (221 BCE-9 CE)
Guanzi.note: Compiled early Han (received text edited by Liu Xiang c. 26 BCE); 'proto-Guanzi' c. 250 BCE; Sato dates most chapters late WS vs Rickett's Han dates for some. Assigned by final compilation.

Guiguzi.label: Late Warring States (c. 300-221 BCE)
Guiguzi.note: Compiled between late WS and end of Han; books I-II reflect genuine WS rhetoric corpus attributed to a 4th-c. teacher; book III a later addition. Least-bad: late WS.

Han_Feizi.label: Late Warring States (c. 300-221 BCE)
Han_Feizi.note: Most of 55 chapters mid-3rd c. BCE; Laozi-commentary chapters 20-21 generally considered later addenda.

Huainanzi.label: Qin-Western Han (221 BCE-9 CE)
Huainanzi.note: Compiled from essays of the court of Liu An, Prince of Huainan, presented to Emperor Wu before 139 BCE; final chapter possibly posthumous.

Kongzi_Jiayu.label: Qin-Western Han (221 BCE-9 CE)
Kongzi_Jiayu.note: Book existed since at least early Han, listed in Yiwenzhi; received version a Wang Su (195-256 CE) recension; Dingzhou/Shuanggudui finds show Han-era material underlying it. Dated as Han compilation.

Laozi.label: Middle Warring States (c. 400-300 BCE)
Laozi.note: Guodian slips c. 300 BCE attest a 4th-c. version; conservative modern estimates put received text mid-3rd c. BCE consolidating older sayings; traditional ascription to a 6th-c. Lao Dan rejected by most. Least-bad: 4th c. BCE.

Liezi.label: Post-Han compilation (3rd-4th c. CE recension, with older layers)
Liezi.note: Many Chinese and Western scholars hold the current text's content was compiled c. 4th c. CE (Zhang Zhan recension); Han-era attestation of a Liezi book and possible WS underlying layers keep dating contested.

Liji.label: Qin-Western Han (221 BCE-9 CE)
Liji.note: Diverse compilation: some chapters pre-Han (Guodian 'Black Robes' c. 300 BCE; parallels in Xunzi, Lushi Chunqiu), others Former Han; received compilation edited by Dai Sheng (Western Han).

Liutao.label: Late Warring States (c. 300-221 BCE)
Liutao.note: Modern historians nominally date final composition to the WS period; some argue vestiges of ancient Qi thought, others a later (Han) compilation; least-bad: late WS.

Lushi_Chunqiu.label: Late Warring States (c. 300-221 BCE)
Lushi_Chunqiu.note: Compiled c. 239 BCE under Lu Buwei; almanac postface dated 239 BCE; other parts completed c. 235 BCE.

Mencius.label: Middle Warring States (c. 400-300 BCE)
Mencius.note: Believed written late 4th c. BCE, largely by disciples of Mencius (c. 371-289).

Mozi.label: Middle Warring States (c. 400-300 BCE)
Mozi.note: Core chapters derive from Mozi (5th c. figure) and early Mohists; 'Dialectical Chapters' patently 3rd c. BCE; 7 chapters of much later date. Assigned by core triads (4th c.).

Shangjunshu.label: Late Warring States (c. 300-221 BCE)
Shangjunshu.note: 3rd-c. BCE text overall (Pines: some chapters from Shang Yang's lifetime or shortly after, composition took over a century, ch. 15 late); earliest Legalist corpus after the attributed layers.

Sima_Fa.label: Middle Warring States (c. 400-300 BCE)
Sima_Fa.note: Developed in Qi during the 4th century BCE (mid-WS), though traditional attribution to Sima Rangju (6th c.) is doubted.

Sunzi_Bingfa.label: Early: Spring and Autumn to early Warring States (pre-c. 400 BCE)
Sunzi_Bingfa.note: Traditionally late Spring and Autumn (c. 5th c. BCE); earliest parts at least a century after the legendary 6th-c. Sun Wu. Significant minority dates it later (WS); least-bad reading: pre-400 BCE core.

Wei_Liaozi.label: Late Warring States (c. 300-221 BCE)
Wei_Liaozi.note: Present form around end of 4th c. BCE; Yinqueshan Han-tomb find confirms pre-Han transmission; authorship (student of Lord Shang vs Qin advisor) unresolved.

Wuzi.label: Middle Warring States (c. 400-300 BCE)
Wuzi.note: No consensus on final composition date; core nominally composed around Wu Qi's lifetime (440-381 BCE), mid-WS.

Xiaojing.label: Late Warring States (c. 300-221 BCE)
Xiaojing.note: Most likely late WS to early Han (4th-3rd c. BCE); assigned to late WS as least-bad reading of the straddling date.

Xunzi.label: Late Warring States (c. 300-221 BCE)
Xunzi.note: Writings of Xun Kuang (3rd c. BCE) and disciples; redacted into 32 bundles by Liu Xiang (1st c. CE).

Zhongyong.label: Qin-Western Han (221 BCE-9 CE)
Zhongyong.note: Traditionally Zisi (5th c. BCE), doubted since Cui Shu; modern scholars hold parts were written/edited at the Qin-Han transition.

Zhuangzi.label: Middle Warring States (c. 400-300 BCE)
Zhuangzi.note: Inner chapters associated with Zhuang Zhou (c. 369-286 BCE); outer/miscellaneous chapters later (school of Zhuangzi, some pre-Han to Han); final compilation Han. Assigned by inner-chapter stratum.

T_ideanat.title: Idealism vs. empiricism/naturalism axis, with pragmatism and philosophy of life as mediating movements
T_ideanat.source_claim: A historiographic partition rather than a single author's scheme: the organizing line of 19th- and early 20th-century philosophy as the confrontation between (transcendental/absolute) idealism and its empiricist-naturalist-positivist critics, with pragmatism and the voluntarist/vitalist 'philosophy of life' as intermediate movements. Codified in John Passmore, A Hundred Years of Philosophy (Duckworth, 1957; reviewed in The Philosophical Review 1959, https://doi.org/10.2307/2182174), the 'revolt against idealism' literature (N. Griffin, 'Russell and Moore's Revolt against British Idealism', Oxford Handbook of Bertrand Russell, 2013, https://doi.org/10.1093/oxfordhb/9780199238842.013.0024), and F. Beiser, Philosophy of Life (OUP, 2023, https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780192899767.001.0001) for the Lebensphilosophie grouping.

Bergson.label: Voluntarism, vitalism and philosophy of life
Bergson.note: Elan vital / creative evolution; Bergson resisted the strict biological sense of 'vitalism', but the label is standard in the literature.

Croce.label: Idealism (transcendental and absolute)
Croce.note: Self-described absolute idealist; his 'philosophy of spirit' is a Hegelian revision.

Eucken.label: Idealism (transcendental and absolute)
Eucken.note: Eucken's 'ethical activism' is an idealist metaphysics of spiritual life explicitly continuous with German idealism (Current History 1916; also Cimino, BJHP 2024); secondary literature is thin, hence medium.

Green.label: Idealism (transcendental and absolute)
Green.note: Neo-Hegelian British absolute idealism ('from Green to Bradley').

Hegel.label: Idealism (transcendental and absolute)
Hegel.note: Absolute idealism takes its canonical form in Hegel.

James.label: Pragmatism
James.note: One of the 'Big Three' pragmatists; his 'radical empiricism' also ties him to the empiricist class.

Kant.label: Idealism (transcendental and absolute)
Kant.note: Transcendental idealism is Kant's own doctrine in the Critique of Pure Reason (Allais 2017).

Kierkegaard.label: Voluntarism, vitalism and philosophy of life
Kierkegaard.note: Fierce critic of Hegelian systematic idealism and forerunner of existentialism; grouped with the anti-rationalist Lebensphilosophie current (Beiser 2023), but he is a Christian existentialist, not a vitalist - placement disputed.

Mach.label: Empiricism, naturalism, positivism and realism
Mach.note: Empiriocriticism; Beiser places him in the positist lineage.

Moore.label: Empiricism, naturalism, positivism and realism
Moore.note: 'Refutation of Idealism' (1903); sense-data realism in the revolt against British idealism (Griffin 2013).

Nietzsche.label: Voluntarism, vitalism and philosophy of life
Nietzsche.note: Standard life-philosophy/voluntarist placement contested by the 'Nietzsche as philosophical naturalist' literature (Janaway & Robertson 2012, https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199583676.003.0001).

Peirce.label: Pragmatism
Peirce.note: Founder ('pragmaticism'); note his self-described scholastic realism, which pulls toward the realist class.

Perry.label: Empiricism, naturalism, positivism and realism
Perry.note: Co-author of The New Realism (1912); standard-bearer of American new realism.

Poincare.label: Empiricism, naturalism, positivism and realism
Poincare.note: Conventionalism as positivist-adjacent philosophy of science (Ben-Menahem 2006); his scientific realism ('no miracles' argument) noted as a tension.

Royce.label: Idealism (transcendental and absolute)
Royce.note: American absolute idealism is standardly identified with Royce (Randall 1966).

Russell.label: Empiricism, naturalism, positivism and realism
Russell.note: Realist revolt against idealism (Griffin 2013); later neutral monism noted.

Santayana.label: Empiricism, naturalism, positivism and realism
Santayana.note: Critical realist (Scepticism and Animal Faith) but a member of the Harvard pragmatist circle who rejected the pragmatist label; placement between the realist and pragmatist classes is disputed.

Schopenhauer.label: Voluntarism, vitalism and philosophy of life
Schopenhauer.note: Transcendental idealist by doctrine (WWR Book I) but founder of the metaphysics of Will leading to Nietzsche; standard histories (e.g. Passmore 1957) group him with voluntarism rather than with Kant/Hegel, so placement is genuinely disputed.

Sidgwick.label: Empiricism, naturalism, positivism and realism
Sidgwick.note: Utilitarian empiricist (Methods of Ethics); intuitionist side-doctrine noted.

Spencer.label: Empiricism, naturalism, positivism and realism
Spencer.note: Evolutionary naturalism of the System of Synthetic Philosophy.

Whitehead.label: Empiricism, naturalism, positivism and realism
Whitehead.note: Philosophy of organism continuous with his mathematical physics and realism about nature, but the speculative metaphysics of Process and Reality is sometimes read as quasi-idealist; placement disputed.

T_lang.title: Confound control partition: works originally written in English vs works translated into English
T_lang.source_claim: Proposed 2026-10-03 by the Six Schools Lab dispatch as the confound-control partition for the sealed-reader study: it is not a philosophical taxonomy but tests whether apparent 'analytic vs continental' separation in the 25-author English corpus (Project Gutenberg texts, pre-1931) is a translation-surface artifact. Theoretical premise: translated prose differs systematically from native prose in vocabulary, syntax and register (translationese), per Gellerstam, 'Fingerprints in Translation' (https://doi.org/10.21832/9781853597893-016), Laviosa, 'Corpus-based Translation Studies' (https://doi.org/10.1163/9789004485907), and Baroni & Bernardini, machine-learning original vs translated text (https://doi.org/10.1093/llc/fqi039). Class assignment rule: written_english if the corpus texts for the author were originally composed in English; translated if originally composed in German, French, Italian, Danish or another language and read in English translation.

Bergson.label: translated
Bergson.note: French philosopher. Creative Evolution is the authorized Arthur Mitchell translation of L'Evolution creatrice (1907), confirmed at https://doi.org/10.5962/bhl.title.166289; Time and Free Will translates Essai sur les donnees immediates de la conscience (1889). Both corpus works are French originals read in English translation.

Bosanquet.label: written_english
Bosanquet.note: English philosopher; The Essentials of Logic and The Philosophical Theory of the State are English originals.

Comte.label: translated
Comte.note: French philosopher; A General View of Positivism is the J.H. Bridges English translation of Discours sur l'ensemble du positivisme (1848).

Croce.label: translated
Croce.note: Italian idealist philosopher; Aesthetic (1902), Logic as the Science of the Pure Concept, and The Philosophy of the Practical are Italian originals read in English translation (Ainslie translations).

Dewey.label: written_english
Dewey.note: American philosopher; all four corpus works (Reconstruction in Philosophy, Essays in Experimental Logic, The Influence of Darwin on Philosophy, Human Nature and Conduct) are English originals.

Eucken.label: translated
Eucken.note: German philosopher (1908 Nobel Prize in Literature); Life's Basis and Life's Ideal and Ethics and Modern Thought are English translations of German works (Grundlinien einer neuen Lebensanschauung; Der Sinn und Wert des Lebens).

Green.label: written_english
Green.note: English philosopher; Lectures on the Principles of Political Obligation comprises his Oxford lectures, published posthumously in English.

Hegel.label: translated
Hegel.note: German philosopher; The Logic of Hegel is William Wallace's translation of the Encyclopaedia Logic, and Philosophy of Mind is Wallace's translation of the Encyclopaedia's Philosophy of Subjective Spirit. Both are German originals read in English translation.

James.label: written_english
James.note: American philosopher; Pragmatism, The Meaning of Truth, A Pluralistic Universe, Essays in Radical Empiricism are English originals (James was fluent in German and French but composed in English).

Kant.label: translated
Kant.note: German philosopher; Critique of Pure Reason, Prolegomena, and Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals are German originals read in English translation.

Kierkegaard.label: translated
Kierkegaard.note: Danish philosopher who wrote in Danish; the corpus unit 'Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard' is an English translation anthology (the 1923 Lee M. Hollander selection). All content is translated from Danish, so the unit is unmixed despite being a compilation; a contemporary review of the volume is at https://doi.org/10.1177/003463733303000418.

Mach.label: translated
Mach.note: Austrian physicist/philosopher; Popular Scientific Lectures is Thomas J. McCormack's English translation of German popular lectures. German original.

Mill.label: written_english
Mill.note: English philosopher; Utilitarianism, A System of Logic, and Auguste Comte and Positivism (Mill's own English-language study of Comte, not a translation) are English originals.

Moore.label: written_english
Moore.note: English philosopher; Principia Ethica and Philosophical Studies are English originals.

Nietzsche.label: translated
Nietzsche.note: German philosopher; all four corpus works (Beyond Good and Evil, The Dawn of Day, The Birth of Tragedy, Human, All Too Human) are German originals read in English translation.

Peirce.label: written_english
Peirce.note: American philosopher; Chance, Love, and Logic (1923) is Morris R. Cohen's posthumous collection of Peirce's English essays and lectures. English originals throughout.

Perry.label: written_english
Perry.note: American philosopher; The Approach to Philosophy and The Moral Economy are English originals.

Poincare.label: translated
Poincare.note: French mathematician/philosopher of science; The Foundations of Science is George Bruce Halsted's English translation of Science and Hypothesis, The Value of Science, and Science and Method. French originals.

Royce.label: written_english
Royce.note: American philosopher; The Sources of Religious Insight is an English original.

Russell.label: written_english
Russell.note: English philosopher; all four corpus works (The Problems of Philosophy, Mysticism and Logic, Our Knowledge of the External World, The Analysis of Mind) are English originals.

Santayana.label: written_english
Santayana.note: Spanish-born but raised and educated in the US from age eight; The Life of Reason, Scepticism and Animal Faith, and Winds of Doctrine are English originals. Native-language status differs from composition language, so this is the one unit where author nativeness and text language diverge; the class rule assigns by composition language.

Schopenhauer.label: translated
Schopenhauer.note: German philosopher; The World as Will and Idea vol. 1 is the Haldane & Kemp English translation of Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung (1818); Studies in Pessimism and The Basis of Morality are English translations of German essays/works.

Sidgwick.label: written_english
Sidgwick.note: English philosopher; The Methods of Ethics is an English original.

Spencer.label: written_english
Spencer.note: English philosopher; First Principles and The Data of Ethics are English originals.

Whitehead.label: written_english
Whitehead.note: English mathematician/philosopher; The Concept of Nature and Science and the Modern World are English originals.

T_literary_form.title: Literary-form partition of early Chinese masters literature (confound control)
T_literary_form.source_claim: A 5-class partition by dominant transmitted literary form, drawn from genre/form studies of pre-Qin and Han texts rather than from Sima Tan's six schools: (1) verse_aphorisms — rhymed aphoristic verse collections (Laozi as consolidating collected sayings in short poetic chapters; Guodian/Mawangdui accretion evidence, Lebovitz 2021 Early China); (2) sayings_dialogues — Analects-type sayings collections in the 'Kongzi said' yu-lu tradition (Poli & Li 2024 Early China) and ruler-master dialogue records (Mencius, Wuzi, Liutao dialogue frames; Xiaojing as Confucius-Zengzi conversation); (3) systematic_treatises — sustained argumentative/doctrinal essays in lun form and systematic military treatises (Xunzi essays; Mozi triads; Han Feizi essays; Sunzi's 13 continuous expository chapters; Pines 2016 on Book of Lord Shang as policy-essay composite); (4) anecdote_anthology_compilations — anecdote/parable collections and heterogeneous or encyclopedic compilations, incl. the miscellany tradition (Heng Du 2020 JAOS), Han ritual compendium (Liji; L'Haridon 2023), Liu Xiang-edited composites (Guanzi, Liezi), and the Zhuangzi's anecdote/allegory/parable-dominant multi-stratal anthology; (5) rhetoric_persuasion_manuals — technical handbooks of persuasion (Guiguzi; Galvany 2012; Conde 2021; cf. Goldin 2020 on persuasion literature). Class-set grounding: Ning Liu, Genres of Chinese Intellectual Thought (2026); Hanmo Zhang, Authorship and Text-making in Early China (2018). Mixed-form books take their dominant transmitted form and are marked contested. Sealed excavated units (Huangdi_Sijing, Sun_Bin_Bingfa) excluded entirely.

Analects.label: sayings_dialogues
Analects.note: Archetypal sayings collection ('zi yue' records) accreted over generations; excavated Zhongni Said / Kongzi Said manuscripts confirm the collection-of-sayings formation process.

Gongsun_Longzi.label: systematic_treatises
Gongsun_Longzi.note: Six extant dialectical essays (lun) on names and actualities from a lost fourteen; the White Horse piece is framed as a debate dialogue but argumentative essay form dominates; some would place it with rhetorical handbooks — medium.

Guanzi.label: anecdote_anthology_compilations
Guanzi.note: Heterogeneous anthology of material from many authors over centuries, compiled/edited by Liu Xiang (76 of 86 chapters survive); mixes essays, verse (Neiye-type) and dialogues — compilation itself is the transmitted form.

Guiguzi.label: rhetoric_persuasion_manuals
Guiguzi.note: Technical manual of persuasion and rhetorical technique (gui/bai, opening/closing, psychological manipulation of interlocutors), distinct from argumentative treatise and anecdote; cf. Conde 2021 (doi:10.17398/1886-9440.15.101).

Han_Feizi.label: systematic_treatises
Han_Feizi.note: 'A selection of essays in the Legalist tradition' (incl. the first Laozi commentaries), but famously rich in anecdotes (Chushuo/Shuolin stores) and contains the persuasion chapter Shuinan; essays dominant — contested.

Huainanzi.label: anecdote_anthology_compilations
Huainanzi.note: 21-essay compiled encyclopedia presented to the Han throne; miscellany-form compendium integrating argument, anecdote, quotation and cosmological system — anthology/compilation.

Kongzi_Jiayu.label: sayings_dialogues
Kongzi_Jiayu.note: 'School Sayings of Confucius': an Analects-type compilation of Confucius sayings, conversations and anecdotes sharing the 'Kongzi said' collection tradition; dominant form is recorded speech.

Laozi.label: verse_aphorisms
Laozi.note: Collection of short rhymed poetic/aphoristic chapters consolidating earlier sayings (Guodian/Mawangdui evidence); the only book in the corpus whose dominant transmitted form is verse.

Liezi.label: anecdote_anthology_compilations
Liezi.note: Eight-chapter compilation of didactic anecdotes, parables and narratives (Liu Xiang redaction; received via Zhang Zhan); anecdote-dominant but with discursive strata — medium.

Liji.label: anecdote_anthology_compilations
Liji.note: Han ritual compendium (L'Haridon): an anthology of heterogeneous ritual records, conversations, narratives and doctrinal chapters (incl. Zhongyong and Daxue) — compilation form.

Liutao.label: sayings_dialogues
Liutao.note: Cast as instruction dictated in dialogue by Tai Gong to Kings Wen and Wu of Zhou (ruler-advisor Q&A frame), yet traditionally classed as a military strategy treatise; mixed — contested.

Lushi_Chunqiu.label: anecdote_anthology_compilations
Lushi_Chunqiu.note: Deliberately structured encyclopedic compilation (ji/lan/lun divisions) integrating argumentative essays with historical anecdotes and quotation; miscellany (zajia) tradition per Heng Du.

Mencius.label: sayings_dialogues
Mencius.note: Conversations with rulers form the basis of the text (dialogue collection), but long sustained argumentative passages (esp. books 3 and 6) approach treatise form; mixed — assigned to dominant dialogue form, hence contested.

Mozi.label: systematic_treatises
Mozi.note: Core is the ten-triad argumentative essays (earliest sustained Chinese treatises), but the received book also contains dialectical canons, anecdotal sections about the master, and technical siege-defense chapters; dominant form is the essay — contested.

Shangjunshu.label: systematic_treatises
Shangjunshu.note: Policy-argumentative essays dominate, but Pines shows a heterogeneous composite text with dialogue-framed chapters and fragmentary aphoristic strata; mixed — contested.

Sima_Fa.label: systematic_treatises
Sima_Fa.note: Terse normative expository prose on military ritual, law and administration (Ban Gu classed it under rites); only 5 of an originally much larger text survive — fragmentary transmission, hence medium.

Sunzi_Bingfa.label: systematic_treatises
Sunzi_Bingfa.note: Thirteen continuous expository chapters each devoted to one aspect of warfare; the archetypal systematic military treatise, no dialogue or anecdote frame.

Wei_Liaozi.label: systematic_treatises
Wei_Liaozi.note: Military-theoretical text: first half theoretical/argumentative chapters, second half terse military-regulation (bingshi) chapters; expository treatise form dominant but internally bipartite — medium.

Wuzi.label: sayings_dialogues
Wuzi.note: Received text is framed as Marquis Wu of Wei asking / Wu Qi answering (ruler-master dialogue), but catalogued among the Seven Military Classics as systematic military doctrine; form (dialogue) vs received characterization (treatise) — contested.

Xiaojing.label: sayings_dialogues
Xiaojing.note: Framed entirely as a Confucius-Zengzi conversation (question-and-answer classic), but transmitted and received as a short doctrinal treatise ('classic treatise'); genuinely mixed form — contested.

Xunzi.label: systematic_treatises
Xunzi.note: Collection of titled argumentative essays (lun-form discussions such as 'Discussion of Heaven', 'Dispelling Obsessions'); the paradigm of the systematic philosophical treatise in the corpus.

Zhongyong.label: systematic_treatises
Zhongyong.note: Transmitted as a discursive doctrinal treatise (traditionally attributed to Zisi; embedded as a Liji chapter), though it opens with a string of 'The Master said' quotations; treatise form dominant.

Zhuangzi.label: anecdote_anthology_compilations
Zhuangzi.note: 'Consists of stories and maxims... many anecdotes, allegories, parables, and fables' — anecdote-dominant, but a multi-stratal anthology (Inner/Outer/Miscellaneous) with dialogue and discursive stretches; mixed — contested.

T_professional_vs_letters.title: The professionalization divide: professional university philosophy (chairs and specialized academic audiences) vs independent man-of-letters philosophy (outside the university, general educated readership)
T_professional_vs_letters.source_claim: Institutional-sociological partition drawn from the intellectual-history literature on the professionalization of philosophy c. 1870-1930: Collini, Public Moralists (Oxford UP 1991) on Britain's shift from generalist public moralists (Mill, Spencer) to specialized academic culture (Green, Sidgwick, the Cambridge/Oxford professoriate); Reuben, The Making of the Modern University (Chicago UP 1996) on the professionalization of American philosophy (James, Dewey, Royce); Ringer, The Decline of the German Mandarins (Harvard UP 1969) on the German professorial mandarinate (Kant-Hegel-Eucken lineage) vs anti-academic modernists (Nietzsche, Schopenhauer's heirs); Hollinger, 'The Problem of Pragmatism in American History' (JAH 1980) on pragmatism's academic professional identity and Peirce's marginality. Criterion: did the author work inside the professional university establishment (chair/fellowship, technical disciplinary audience), or as an independent writer for the general educated public?

Bergson.label: Professional university philosophy
Bergson.note: Contested: held the College de France chair (1900-14), but was a celebrity bestseller read by the general public and 1927 Nobel laureate in literature, often grouped with anti-academic philosophy of life.

Bosanquet.label: Professional university philosophy
Bosanquet.note: Contested: resigned his Oxford fellowship in 1881 and held no chair, yet remained a leader of the academic neo-Hegelian establishment (Aristotelian Society president 1894-98, Gifford Lecturer).

Comte.label: Independent man-of-letters philosophy
Comte.note: Dismissed from his Ecole Polytechnique examiner post in 1844; thereafter lived on patronage and subscriptions as an independent positivist lecturer and founder of a lay church.

Croce.label: Independent man-of-letters philosophy
Croce.note: Never held a university chair; independent intellectual working from his Neapolitan palazzo, editing La Critica and serving as senator - the European model of the lay philosopher.

Dewey.label: Professional university philosophy
Dewey.note: Chairs at Michigan, Chicago, Columbia; Reuben and Hollinger both place him at the core of the professionalized academic discipline.

Eucken.label: Professional university philosophy
Eucken.note: Contested: Jena philosophy professor and Ringer-style mandarin, yet wrote popular Lebensphilosophie for a mass educated readership and won the 1908 Nobel Prize in LITERATURE.

Green.label: Professional university philosophy
Green.note: White's Professor of Moral Philosophy at Oxford (1878); Collini's exemplar of the public moralist tradition passing INTO the universities in the 1870s.

Hegel.label: Professional university philosophy
Hegel.note: Chairs at Heidelberg (1816) and Berlin (1818); philosophy as a state-salaried professorial science.

James.label: Professional university philosophy
James.note: Harvard professor of psychology then philosophy (1876-1907); institutionally a professional even where his style remained literary.

Kant.label: Professional university philosophy
Kant.note: Ordentlicher Professor at Koenigsberg from 1770; the archetypal salaried university philosopher who created the model Ringer's mandarins later inhabited.

Kierkegaard.label: Independent man-of-letters philosophy
Kierkegaard.note: Private gentleman-scholar on an inheritance; never held a university post, published under pseudonyms and addressed the reading public and the church, not the academy.

Mach.label: Professional university philosophy
Mach.note: University professor (Prague physics; Vienna chair of history and theory of inductive science 1895-1901); a university professional on this institutional axis even though his discipline was physics.

Mill.label: Independent man-of-letters philosophy
Mill.note: East India Company administrator, MP and journalist; Collini's archetypal Victorian 'public moralist' who philosophized for the general reading public, never holding an academic post.

Moore.label: Professional university philosophy
Moore.note: Cambridge fellow and Professor of Mental Philosophy and Logic; paradigm of the specialized academic analytic style.

Nietzsche.label: Independent man-of-letters philosophy
Nietzsche.note: Contested: Basel professor of classical philology 1869-79, but resigned the chair and wrote aphoristically for a general audience; Ringer treats him as the anti-academic 'modernist' pole against the German mandarinate.

Peirce.label: Independent man-of-letters philosophy
Peirce.note: Contested: America's greatest logician yet professionally marginal - thirty years a Coast Survey scientist with only a five-year Johns Hopkins lectureship; Hollinger and Menand-style accounts stress his exclusion from the professional academy.

Perry.label: Professional university philosophy
Perry.note: Harvard professor of philosophy; official biographer of James and product of the professional graduate system.

Poincare.label: Professional university philosophy
Poincare.note: Professor at the Sorbonne and Academie des Sciences member; his popularizations (Science et hypothese) were written from inside the professorial scientific establishment.

Royce.label: Professional university philosophy
Royce.note: Harvard professor of philosophy; central figure in Reuben's account of American philosophy's professionalization at Chicago/Harvard.

Russell.label: Professional university philosophy
Russell.note: Trinity College Cambridge fellow and lecturer; his popular essays and 1950 Nobel Prize in Literature sit uneasily with the class but his working identity was the academic profession.

Santayana.label: Independent man-of-letters philosophy
Santayana.note: Contested: Harvard professor 1889-1912, then resigned and lived as an expatriate independent man of letters (novelist, poet, essayist) supported by royalties.

Schopenhauer.label: Independent man-of-letters philosophy
Schopenhauer.note: Contested: held a Berlin Privatdozent license (1820) but lived off his inheritance outside the university and famously attacked 'professorial philosophy' (On University Professors of Philosophy).

Sidgwick.label: Professional university philosophy
Sidgwick.note: Knightbridge Professor of Moral Philosophy, Cambridge; technical academic ethics written for the specialized Moral Sciences readership.

Spencer.label: Independent man-of-letters philosophy
Spencer.note: Full-time independent author supported by subscribers and sales; the paradigmatic freelance system-builder in Collini's account of pre-professional intellectual culture.

Whitehead.label: Professional university philosophy
Whitehead.note: Cambridge lecturer/fellow then Harvard professor of philosophy (1924); fully inside the university establishment.

T_retro.title: Retrospective Analytic-Continental Division (post-1945 usage) applied to 25 pre-1931 authors
T_retro.source_claim: The 'analytic vs continental' division of philosophy became standard only after 1945 (Russell himself drew a two-schools contrast in 1945; the term 'continental philosophy' in its current sense spread among English-speaking philosophers from the 1970s). Key documentations: Dummett, Origins of Analytical Philosophy (1993, reviewed J. Phil. 1995, https://doi.org/10.5840/jphil1995921010); Critchley, Continental Philosophy: A Very Short Introduction (OUP 2001, https://doi.org/10.1093/actrade/9780192853592.001.0001), esp. ch.2 'Origins of Continental Philosophy: How to get from Kant to German Idealism' (https://doi.org/10.1093/actrade/9780192853592.003.0002); Glock, What is Analytic Philosophy? (CUP 2008, https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9780511841125); surveys at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_philosophy and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_philosophy. This taxonomy applies that retrospective sorting to the 25 pre-1931 corpus authors, with a third class for pragmatists and other figures the post-war literature treats as neither/precursors.

Bergson.label: Continental (retrospective attribution)
Bergson.note: Standard retrospective sorting places Bergson with continental philosophy (revived by Deleuze's 1966 Le Bergsonisme); he was the explicit target of Russell's and Carnap's critiques, defining the analytic side against him.

Bosanquet.label: Continental (retrospective attribution)
Bosanquet.note: Leading British absolute idealist (with Green and Bradley); same rationale as Green - Hegelian lineage, the foil of early analytic philosophy.

Comte.label: Neither: pragmatism and other traditions outside the divide
Comte.note: CONTESTED: founder of positivism, ancestor-figure of logical positivism (analytic side), but French and canonized by neither camp - continental histories treat positivism as what 'continental' defines itself against while analytic histories start later; he falls outside both retrospective canons.

Croce.label: Continental (retrospective attribution)
Croce.note: Italian idealist in the Hegelian lineage; sorted under the Hegelian-idealist umbrella of continental histories (Critchley 2001), though Italy's place in that canon is secondary.

Dewey.label: Neither: pragmatism and other traditions outside the divide
Dewey.note: Co-founder of pragmatism; same third-tradition placement as James.

Eucken.label: Continental (retrospective attribution)
Eucken.note: German idealist 'life-philosophy' (Nobel 1908); fits the German Idealist-to-Lebensphilosophie lineage the continental narrative retraces, but is marginal in post-war sorting.

Green.label: Continental (retrospective attribution)
Green.note: Leading British idealist; British idealism 'developed from the German idealist movement - particularly Kant and Hegel' and is the movement analytic philosophy was founded against, so the retrospective divide sorts it with the idealist (continental) side despite geography.

Hegel.label: Continental (retrospective attribution)
Hegel.note: German Idealism is the canonical continental lineage; Hegelianism is named first among the traditions 'continental' covers (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_philosophy).

James.label: Neither: pragmatism and other traditions outside the divide
James.note: Co-founder of pragmatism; classical American pragmatism is standardly treated as a third tradition, not a branch of either analytic or continental.

Kant.label: Continental (retrospective attribution)
Kant.note: Critchley's standard continental history starts the lineage at Kant and runs to German Idealism; Kant is the retrospective origin point of 'continental'.

Kierkegaard.label: Continental (retrospective attribution)
Kierkegaard.note: Named explicitly as an antecedent of existentialism within continental philosophy.

Mach.label: Analytic (retrospective attribution)
Mach.note: Austrian philosopher of science, 'a major influence on logical positivism'; logical positivism is inside the analytic lineage (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_philosophy). Placed as proto-positivist precursor, not analytic proper.

Mill.label: Analytic (retrospective attribution)
Mill.note: CONTESTED: Mill is a Victorian empiricist/utilitarian who predates the split; he himself first contrasted 'Continental philosophy' with English empiricism (1840 essay on Coleridge), and the British-idealist movement defined itself against Mill and Sidgwick (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_idealism); but Dummett's origins-of-analytic narrative starts from Frege/Brentano, not Mill, so the retrospective claim of Mill for 'analytic' is disputed.

Moore.label: Analytic (retrospective attribution)
Moore.note: Central founder figure alongside Russell; the rejection of British idealism begins with Moore and Russell.

Nietzsche.label: Continental (retrospective attribution)
Nietzsche.note: CONTESTED: canonically sorted continental as an existentialist antecedent, but the literature disputes how cleanly he fits any school of the divide - his strong transatlantic/American reception complicates the sorting (Krell, 'Emerson-Nietzsche's Voluptuary?', https://doi.org/10.1179/1757063815z.00000000045).

Peirce.label: Neither: pragmatism and other traditions outside the divide
Peirce.note: CONTESTED: 'father of pragmatism' (a distinct third tradition per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pragmatism), yet also claimed by the analytic lineage as 'America's greatest logician' whose semiotics 'foreshadowed the debate among logical positivists' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Sanders_Peirce; Rydenfelt, 'Pragmatism and analytic philosophy', https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315149592-23).

Perry.label: Neither: pragmatism and other traditions outside the divide
Perry.note: American critical realist and naturalist of the Harvard pragmatist circle (editor of James); belongs to the classical American tradition outside the divide.

Poincare.label: Analytic (retrospective attribution)
Poincare.note: French mathematician-philosopher of science; conventionalism was taken up by logical empiricism, so the post-war literature sorts him with the precursors of the analytic side rather than with Bergson-style French philosophy.

Royce.label: Neither: pragmatism and other traditions outside the divide
Royce.note: 'American pragmatist and absolute idealist... founder of American idealism' - the post-war literature sorts him into classical American philosophy, claimed by neither the analytic nor the continental camp cleanly.

Russell.label: Analytic (retrospective attribution)
Russell.note: Central founder figure in every history of analytic philosophy; his rebellion against neo-Hegelianism with Moore is the standard origin story.

Santayana.label: Neither: pragmatism and other traditions outside the divide
Santayana.note: Classical American philosopher of the pragmatist generation; standard retrospective sorting leaves him outside both camps (pragmatist-adjacent, critical of both idealism and naturalized empiricism).

Schopenhauer.label: Continental (retrospective attribution)
Schopenhauer.note: Philosophical pessimism is explicitly listed among the continental traditions in the standard survey.

Sidgwick.label: Analytic (retrospective attribution)
Sidgwick.note: Empiricist/utilitarian whom British idealism reacted against; his Methods of Ethics is retrospectively claimed as a precursor of analytic ethics, though he predates the linguistic turn.

Spencer.label: Neither: pragmatism and other traditions outside the divide
Spencer.note: Victorian evolutionary system-builder; hugely read pre-1931 but the post-1945 literature of both analytic and continental camps largely dropped him - a precursor to neither side's self-narrative. No single standard history claims him; citation uncertain.

Whitehead.label: Neither: pragmatism and other traditions outside the divide
Whitehead.note: CONTESTED: co-author of Principia Mathematica (foundational for analytic logic) yet his later process metaphysics 'radically departed from most of Western philosophy'; the post-1945 literature treats him as outside the analytic mainstream and he is often read as neither/n precursor of both.

T_six.title: Sima Tan's six schools (Lun liujia yaozhi, Shiji 130): Yin-Yang, Confucian, Mohist, Names, Legalist, Daoist
T_six.source_claim: Six-fold partition of the early Chinese masters proposed by Sima Tan (Grand Astrologer, d. 110 BCE) in his essay 'Lun liujia yaozhi' (論六家要旨), preserved in Shiji ch. 130 (Taishigong zixu), completed by his son Sima Qian ca. 91 BCE; Tan's essay names yinyang jia, ru jia, mo jia, ming jia, fa jia and dao jia (documented at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sima_Tan and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Schools_of_Thought). This taxonomy transfers Tan's six labels onto the 23 transmitted books of the corpus, following the Han bibliographic tradition (Hanshu Yiwenzhi; context in Hunter 2019, https://doi.org/10.7817/jameroriesoci.138.4.0763) and standard sinological reference works. Books that Han bibliography placed in categories OUTSIDE the six schools (military/bing, ritual canon, Zajia eclectics, Zongheng diplomacy) are force-assigned to the least-bad class and marked contested; the Yin-Yang class receives no book because its central figure Zou Yan's writings are all lost (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zou_Yan).

Analects.label: Confucian
Analects.note: Sayings of Confucius compiled by his followers; by the end of Han 'a central text of Confucianism' (origin account via Ban Gu, Book of Han); core ru jia text.

Gongsun_Longzi.label: Names
Gongsun_Longzi.note: Gongsun Long (c. 320-250 BC) was 'a member of the School of Names' (Logicians/Sophists); his collected works comprise the Gongsun Longzi anthology (White Horse dialogue, 'white horses are not horses').

Guanzi.label: Daoist
Guanzi.note: CONTESTED: the Hanshu Yiwenzhi classifies the Guanzi under the Daoist school (道家類), the Suishu Jingjizhi reclassified it under the Legalist school (法家類), and modern scholarship (Rickett; Sato) treats it as a syncretic Jixia composite with strong Legalist, Confucian and Huang-Lao/Neiye layers (English overview: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guanzi_(text)); assigned Daoist per the earliest, Han-dynasty classification.

Guiguzi.label: Daoist
Guiguzi.note: CONTESTED: 'originally associated with the School of Diplomacy' (Zongheng jia, the persuaders' school of Su Qin and Zhang Yi), which is not one of the six schools, but the text 'was later integrated into the Daoist canon'; least-bad six-school class = Daoist.

Han_Feizi.label: Legalist
Han_Feizi.note: 'A selection of essays in the Legalist tradition'; often considered the culminating Legalist text (A.C. Graham's 'great synthesizer' of Legalism).

Huainanzi.label: Daoist
Huainanzi.note: CONTESTED: 'Confucian bibliographers classified it as Zajia (Syncretist), but came to often consider it a Taoist classic'; K.C. Hsiao and the work's modern translators consider it a principal example of Han Taoism (Huang-Lao synthesis subverting Confucian, Mohist and Legalist material toward a less active ruler); assigned Daoist.

Kongzi_Jiayu.label: Confucian
Kongzi_Jiayu.note: Sayings of Confucius written as a supplement to the Analects; listed in the 1st-century imperial bibliography (Yiwenzhi) with 27 scrolls; received text long dismissed as Wang Su's 3rd-c. compilation, partially rehabilitated by Dingzhou (55 BC) and Shuanggudui (165 BC) finds; school identity Confucian.

Laozi.label: Daoist
Laozi.note: 'Regarded as the foundational Taoist text'; the dao jia core text (Guodian fragments c. 300 BCE, received text consolidated by mid-3rd c. BCE).

Liezi.label: Daoist
Liezi.note: CONTESTED: the Hanshu bibliography knew an 8-pian Liezi and Tang canonization made it a Daoist classic alongside Laozi and Zhuangzi, but many Chinese and Western scholars hold the received text is a compilation of ca. 4th c. CE (Zhang Zhan redaction); school placement Daoist, textual dating and authenticity disputed.

Liji.label: Confucian
Liji.note: CONTESTED: composite ritual anthology of uncertain Warring States-Han origin, canonized as one of the Confucian Five Classics ('a core Confucian text'); as a ritual classic it belongs to the canon category rather than a masters' school, so the Confucian assignment rests on canonization, not school authorship.

Liutao.label: Daoist
Liutao.note: CONTESTED: Seven Military Classics strategist text attributed to Taigong/Jiang Ziya (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six_Secret_Teachings); no natural six-school class; the Hanshu Yiwenzhi is traditionally said to group the Taigong corpus under the Daoist school, but no citable URL for that placement was retrievable from the lab's research tools, hence 'uncertain'; least-bad class = Daoist.

Lushi_Chunqiu.label: Daoist
Lushi_Chunqiu.note: CONTESTED: Han bibliography classes this 239 BCE Qin court compendium as Zajia/Syncretist (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lüshi_Chunqiu), a category outside Sima Tan's six; zh-wiki characterizes it as Huang-Lao Daoist-dominant (以道家黃老思想為主) while the Siku quanshu editors read it as Confucian-dominant (大抵以儒為主); least-bad six-school class = Daoist.

Mencius.label: Confucian
Mencius.note: Anthology of the Confucian philosopher Mencius (c. 371-289 BC); 'one of the most important texts that explores the philosophy of Confucianism', developing Confucius's doctrines.

Mozi.label: Mohist
Mozi.note: 'Expounds the philosophy of Mohism' (impartial care, meritocracy, anti-ostentation, defensive warfare); the mo jia core text.

Shangjunshu.label: Legalist
Shangjunshu.note: 'Regarded as a foundational work of Chinese Legalism'; earliest surviving Legalist text, associated with Qin reformer Shang Yang; listed as 'Lord Shang' 29 pian in the Book of Han catalogue.

Sima_Fa.label: Confucian
Sima_Fa.note: CONTESTED: a Seven Military Classics text on military administration, but 'in the East Han dynasty, The Methods of the Sima was classified as a work describing rites and propriety (li), by Ban Gu', filing it with the ritual/Confucian tradition; least-bad six-school class = Confucian.

Sunzi_Bingfa.label: Daoist
Sunzi_Bingfa.note: CONTESTED: a Seven Military Classics strategist text (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Art_of_War); the Hanshu catalogue filed Sun Wu under the military (bing) category, outside the six schools; the literature describes its philosophy as combining 'a Daoist philosophy of inaction and impartiality' with a Legalist system of rewards and punishments; least-bad class = Daoist.

Wei_Liaozi.label: Legalist
Wei_Liaozi.note: CONTESTED: Seven Military Classics text; Wei Liao is 'said to have either been a student of Lord Shang or an important advisor during the Qin dynasty', and the text punishes heterodoxy 'using draconian measures' while advocating humanistic government; the Hanshu catalogue knew two works of this name (one in the military category); least-bad class = Legalist per the Lord Shang linkage and law-centered statecraft.

Wuzi.label: Legalist
Wuzi.note: CONTESTED: 'the philosophical content of the work mainly consists of a synthesis between Confucianism and Legalism' - Wu Qi trained three years as a Confucian student and frames the army as guardian of benevolence and righteousness, but the text's operative doctrine is strict rewards and punishments (zh-wiki: 賞罰嚴明，進有重賞，退有重刑, https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/吳子); assigned Legalist as the operative administrative doctrine.

Xiaojing.label: Confucian
Xiaojing.note: 'A Confucian classic treatise' on filial piety (late Warring States-early Han; author unknown, framed as Confucius-Zengzi dialogue); medium confidence because it is a classic-category text whose school identity, though unambiguous, rests on canonical tradition.

Xunzi.label: Confucian
Xunzi.note: Writings of Xun Kuang, 'a 3rd-century BC philosopher usually associated with the Confucian tradition'; he influenced Legalist students (Han Fei) but his school label is ru jia.

Zhongyong.label: Confucian
Zhongyong.note: Originally a Liji chapter attributed to Zisi, grandson of Confucius; 'a central doctrine of Confucianism' and one of the Four Books; authorship debated (possible Qin-Han Confucian editing) but the school identity is unambiguous.

Zhuangzi.label: Daoist
Zhuangzi.note: 'One of the two foundational texts of Taoism' alongside the Tao Te Ching.

T_yiwenzhi_nine.title: Liu Xin / Ban Gu nine-streams scheme (Hanshu Yiwenzhi, early 1st c. CE)
T_yiwenzhi_nine.source_claim: Proposed by Liu Xin (Qilue, c. late 1st c. BCE - 23 CE) and preserved by Ban Gu in the Yiwenzhi bibliographic treatise (Hanshu ch. 30, by 111 CE), which organizes all known literature into six divisions and whose 'Zhuzi lüe' defines the ten schools / nine streams (jiuliu shijia). Documented at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yiwenzhi and https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/藝文志 ('九流十家'一詞便出自《漢書藝文志略序》); studied in Hunter 2019, JAOS, https://doi.org/10.7817/jameroriesoci.138.4.0763. Each book is placed in the Yiwenzhi category where the catalog records it; least-best-fit assignments marked contested. Sealed excavated units (Huangdi_Sijing, Sun_Bin_Bingfa) are excluded entirely and receive no label.

Analects.label: Six Arts (Liujia)
Analects.note: The Yiwenzhi catalogs the Lunyu in the Six Arts division as its own appended class (not under the masters); the treatise's six-domain system derives from Liu Xin's Qilüe per the cited article.

Gongsun_Longzi.label: School of Names (Mingjia)
Gongsun_Longzi.note: Yiwenzhi Mingjia section: Gongsun Longzi 14 pian (6 essays extant); cited article confirms Gongsun Long as member of the School of Names (Logicians).

Guanzi.label: Daoists (Daojia)
Guanzi.note: zh Wikipedia states explicitly that the Hanshu Yiwenzhi lists the Guanzi under Daojia, with reclassification to Fajia only in the Suishu jingjizhi. This surprising placement is exactly as the Han catalog recorded it.

Guiguzi.label: Strategists (Zonghengjia)
Guiguzi.note: NOT recorded in the Hanshu Yiwenzhi; first cataloged under zongheng (School of Diplomacy) in the Sui-period jingjizhi (the zh 藝文志 article notes the zongheng category gained the Guiguzi only later). Least-best fit: Strategists (Zonghengjia), the Yiwenzhi category for Su Qin / Zhang Yi persuasion literature to which the Guiguzi tradition belongs; contested because the book eludes the Han catalog and its dating/attribution are disputed.

Han_Feizi.label: Legalists (Fajia)
Han_Feizi.note: Yiwenzhi Fajia section: Hanzi (Han Feizi) 55 pian; cited article confirms the text as the synthesizer of Fajia thought.

Huainanzi.label: Eclectics (Zajia)
Huainanzi.note: Yiwenzhi Zajia section: Huainan nei 21 pian; cited article confirms Han bibliographers classified it as Zajia (Syncretist), its Daoist reputation being largely later.

Kongzi_Jiayu.label: Confucians (Rujia)
Kongzi_Jiayu.note: The Yiwenzhi does record a Kongzi Jiayu (27 juan), transmitted within the Confucian (Rujia) tradition; however the received 10-juan/44-section text is associated with Wang Su (3rd c. CE) and long deemed a forgery, its status only partially rehabilitated by the Dingzhou and Shuanggudui finds. Contested because the received text's relation to the Yiwenzhi entry is disputed.

Laozi.label: Daoists (Daojia)
Laozi.note: Yiwenzhi zhuzi lüe, Daojia section (Laozi with Han commentaries/transmissions); anchor article documents the Daojia category of the Yiwenzhi.

Liezi.label: Daoists (Daojia)
Liezi.note: Yiwenzhi Daojia section records Liezi 8 pian; but the received text is by many scholars considered a 4th-c. CE compilation (Zhang Zhan tradition), so the received book's identity with the Yiwenzhi entry is disputed.

Liji.label: Six Arts (Liujia)
Liji.note: Recorded in the Yiwenzhi Six Arts division under the Li class (Ji 131 pian, the Records corpus of which the received Liji is the transmitted portion); cited article confirms its status as the ritual classic of the Five Classics.

Liutao.label: Daoists (Daojia)
Liutao.note: The Liutao is not separately titled in the Yiwenzhi; the catalog registers the parent Taigong corpus (237 pian: mou 81, yan 71, bing 85 - the bing portion corresponding to the Liutao) under the DAOJIA section, not the military division. Least-best fit faithful to the Han catalog: Daoists; contested because the received Liutao's equation with the Yiwenzhi Taigong-bing portion rests on the standard reading of Hanshu ch. 30 (cf. https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/藝文志) but no tool-verified URL stated it explicitly, and later catalogs (Sui onward) treat the Liutao as a military classic.

Lushi_Chunqiu.label: Eclectics (Zajia)
Lushi_Chunqiu.note: Yiwenzhi Zajia section: Lüshi chunqiu 26 pian; cited article confirms traditional 'Syncretist' (Zajia) classification.

Mencius.label: Confucians (Rujia)
Mencius.note: Recorded in the Yiwenzhi zhuzi lüe, Rujia section (Mengzi 11 pian); the cited article confirms it as a Confucian anthology, canonized as a classic only later (Song).

Mozi.label: Mohists (Mojia)
Mozi.note: Yiwenzhi zhuzi lüe, Mojia section: Mozi 71 pian; uncontroversial placement in the catalog that defines the nine streams.

Shangjunshu.label: Legalists (Fajia)
Shangjunshu.note: Yiwenzhi Fajia section: Shangjun 29 pian; uncontroversial catalog placement.

Sima_Fa.label: Six Arts (Liujia)
Sima_Fa.note: Cited article: in the Eastern Han the Sima Fa was classified by Ban Gu as a work of rites and propriety (li) - i.e., the Yiwenzhi registers it as junli Sima Fa (military ritual) in the Li class of the Six Arts division, NOT in the military division; its bingjia classification is later. Medium confidence because the received text is a remnant of the 155-pian original.

Sunzi_Bingfa.label: Military Works (Bingshu)
Sunzi_Bingfa.note: Yiwenzhi Military division (Bingshu lüe), strategy section (bing quanmou): Wu Sunzi bingfa 82 pian (13-chapter core received); the military division is one of the Yiwenzhi's six, outside the masters lüe.

Wei_Liaozi.label: Military Works (Bingshu)
Wei_Liaozi.note: The Yiwenzhi records TWO works of this name: Weiliao 31 pian under the Eclectics (Zajia) and Weiliaozi 29 pian under the Military division; cited article confirms two different works of the same name were known in the Han. Least-best fit: Military Works (following the majority identification of the received text with the 29-pian military entry, supported by the 1972 Yinqueshan find among military texts); contested because of the dual listing.

Wuzi.label: Military Works (Bingshu)
Wuzi.note: Yiwenzhi Military division (bing quanmou): Wu Qi 48 pian; cited article confirms the Wuzi as Wu Qi's military treatise later canonized among the Seven Military Classics.

Xiaojing.label: Six Arts (Liujia)
Xiaojing.note: The Yiwenzhi gives the Xiaojing its own class within the Six Arts division; cited article confirms its status as a Confucian classic treatise used in Han education.

Xunzi.label: Confucians (Rujia)
Xunzi.note: Yiwenzhi Rujia section records Sun Qingzi (Xunzi) 33 pian; the anchor article documents the Yiwenzhi as the source catalog of the nine-streams scheme.

Zhongyong.label: Six Arts (Liujia)
Zhongyong.note: The Yiwenzhi knows the Zhongyong only as material of the Records (Ji 131 pian) and a Zhongyong shuo (2 pian) within the Six Arts/Li class; separate-book status is a later (Tang/Song) development. Cited article confirms it was originally a chapter of the Liji.

Zhuangzi.label: Daoists (Daojia)
Zhuangzi.note: Yiwenzhi Daojia section: Zhuangzi 52 pian (received text has 33); uncontroversial.

preregistration.registered_by: human (team), drafted with a coding assistant; fixed before any lab run
preregistration.registered_at: 2026-10-03T17:20:00-07:00 (plan v2); frozen in git before the first Omnigent session
preregistration.objective: Audit inherited taxonomies of thought: is a taxonomy a structure already present in the texts (discovered) or a label imposed later (invented)? Use two leak-free designs: a sealed text (Mawangdui manuscript, buried 168 BCE) and a sealed reader (a language model trained only on pre-1931 text).

defector_targets.note: Advocates must name the Daoist and Legalist classes exactly 'Daoist' and 'Legalist' in the six-schools taxonomy.

H-C1.claim: The six-schools taxonomy predicts where an unseen book falls better than era, region or genre taxonomies.
H-C1.decision: rank by chance-corrected score with 95% bootstrap interval; require agreement across instruments (lex, lex_tr) for a main claim

H-C2.claim: The instrument ranks chapters that scholars regard as Daoist-leaning (Guanzi: Neiye, Xinshu I-II, Baixin; Han Feizi: Jie Lao, Yu Lao) high on Daoist affinity within their own books.
H-C2.decision: PASS if mean target percentile >= 80 and permutation p < 0.05; otherwise the instrument fails validation and no main conclusion may be published

H-C3.claim: The sealed manuscript sits between Dao and Fa instead of falling cleanly into one school.
H-C3.decision: 'constructed' prediction holds if dominant label share < 0.70 OR mean margin below the 10th percentile of transmitted books; otherwise the 'real structure' prediction holds

H-W1.claim: A reader sealed in 1930 already separates what was later called analytic vs continental philosophy.

H-W2.claim: A modern reader separates the later label more sharply than the 1930 reader, beyond its general advantage on labels that already existed in 1930 (hindsight gap G > 0).

decision_rules_after_first_tournament: If the six-schools taxonomy leads AND the tomb test supports 'real structure': next experiment = extend the sealed-text test to the Guodian slips.

If the six-schools taxonomy leads BUT the tomb test supports 'constructed': rewrite the conclusion as 'school structure holds in Han-edited transmitted books but not out of sample'; prioritise the translation-arm rerun.
If an era, region or genre taxonomy leads: reopen the premise that the school is the basic unit; next experiment = school test within era strata.

conclusion.title: Six-schools lab final conclusion - PHASE 1 (sealed text, zh) + PHASE 2 (sealed reader, en)
conclusion.auditor_signoff: r0165 - FIT FOR PUBLICATION, zero required changes; number verification PASS (every number matches its cited record)
conclusion.credits: 16/16 used; no further runs executed; every number quoted from executed result/evidence records

H-C1.verdict: REFUTED as pre-registered in run A (no main superiority claim); narrow finding survives (six beats its own null). The tie central to the refutation DID NOT REPLICATE in run B; cross-run robustness of six-vs-form not established in either direction.
H-C1.numbers: Run A lex chance-corrected: six 0.3539 (p=0.0005, r0063) ~ genre 0.3359 (p=0.0005, r0069) > region 0.2592 (p=0.002, r0067) > yiwenzhi 0.2437 (p=0.001, r0103) > era 0.0996 (p=0.18 n.s., r0065); lex_tr rank flip genre 0.3544 (p=0.0005, r0079) > six 0.3272 (p=0.002, r0077). Run B (via human evidence r0154, record sha cef46d81... at its r0064): six 0.486 (p=0.0005, 21/25), yiwenzhi_nine 0.328, literary_form 0.261 (p=0.01), era -0.06 (p=0.7), six-no-military 0.579. Han-editorial circularity not supported; form/register confound is the LEADING interpretation, not demonstrated (r0110/r0117).
H-C1.detail_record: r0158 - stored payload permanently budget-truncated after 'T_literary_form 0.261'; complete run-B H-C1 figures in r0159/r0162 (disclosed per r0165 advisory)

H-C2.verdict: SUPPORTED - instruments validated; the lab's strongest and only cleanly replicated substantive result. Validates the instruments, not the taxonomy; scope zh lex/lex_tr only (no en-instrument validation ever run).
H-C2.numbers: Run A defectors(six): lex mean target percentile 95.40 (p~1e-4, r0056), lex_tr 97.14 (p~1e-4, r0058). Run B: lex 95.0, lex_tr 96.8 (p=0.0001, r0154). REPLICATED across runs.

H-C3.verdict: SUPPORTED in run A per the pre-registered rule ('constructed' branch) with mandatory calibration caveats; DID NOT REPLICATE in run B. Must not be relied on as established.
H-C3.numbers: Run A: dominant Daoist share 0.588 (10/17, r0071) and stripped 0.647 (11/17, r0090/r0091), both < 0.70 threshold; percentiles 56.5/60.9; ~39% of transmitted books also fall below 0.70 (threshold miscalibrated, r0092); Wilson 95% CI for stripped 11/17 [0.413, 0.827] spans 0.70 (baseline ~[0.360, 0.784] also spans); lex_tr tomb run deferred, never executed (r0101). Run B: shares Daoist 0.824 / Legalist 0.176, margin percentile 87 - cleanly Daoist (r0154).

H-W1.verdict: NOT SUPPORTED as pre-registered; on the underlying doctrinal question UNDECIDED pending decisive test C1 - neither demonstrated nor refuted.
H-W1.numbers: Pre-registered rule (r0134/r0135): condition (i) MET - T_retro x talkie accuracy 0.4831 vs null 0.2430 (sd 0.0763), z=3.147, p_perm=0.0015, cc=0.3171, 21/25 testable (r0139/r0145). Condition (ii) FAILED numerically - T_translated x talkie cc=0.7547 (0.8782 vs 0.5034, p=0.0005, 25/25; r0141/r0146), T_nation x talkie cc=0.5255 (0.5902 vs 0.1364, p=0.0005, 22/25; r0143/r0147) - but per skeptic r0152 AE2 the cross-taxonomy cc comparison is ill-posed as subsumption evidence. Substantive basis is AE1 (re-verified against r0139): a translation-status-only oracle achieves accuracy 0.476 / cc~0.308 - the CEILING of any such rule - vs observed 0.483/0.317, indistinguishable; within Continental, translated members mean 0.769 vs original-English 0.111 (Bosanquet/Green/Royce at floor 0.133/0.133/0.067); survives masked=true.
H-W1.surviving_claim: A reader sealed in 1930 places unseen authors on the retrospective grid above chance; leading (not demonstrated) interpretation is translationese/provenance mimicry.

H-W2.verdict: NOT TESTABLE AS DESIGNED (skeptic correction r0152 AE3 adopted in r0155); on its face also not established - bootstrap CI straddles zero.
H-W2.numbers: G = +0.0242, bootstrap 95% CI [-0.0280, +0.0782]; retro_advantage_of_modern +0.0277; contemporary_advantage_of_modern +0.0035; n=21 per side; layer=mid (r0137). Estimand confounded: 4-class T_retro vs 8-class T_1930 with different author sets; tool returned deltas only - the four absolute LOAO cells never exposed and unauditable (r0144); qwen-translationese channel untested (needs r0153 C2/C4). Kant limitation note carried per auditor condition (r0149). No PHASE 2 replication exists.

replication_across_runs.source: Human evidence r0154; run B = second lab run, own record (sha cef46d817e06315d92e4e7f202cb727086502c26d400aaa9aeb48c4804d37c31 at its r0064), vendors swapped, no fixed protocol, strip_lacunae always on.

Six-schools beats its own permutation null (A: 0.3539, p=0.0005, r0063; B: 0.486, p=0.0005)
Era taxonomy has no predictive power (A: 0.0996, p=0.18, r0065; B: -0.06, p=0.7)
not_replicated: Six vs literary form: tied in run A (0.354 vs 0.336, r0063/r0069, plus lex_tr flip r0077/r0079); six clearly ahead in run B (0.486 vs 0.261)

replication_across_runs.reading: Both non-replications trace to the advocates' coding of the six-schools and form taxonomies (operator reading in r0154, explicitly input for planner and auditor, not a conclusion). Run B is a conceptual, not strict-protocol, replication. PHASE 2 (en) has no independent replication.

process_disclosures.recognition_probe: Probe numbers cited exclusively from the definitive rerun r0111/r0112/r0113: prober_a 33/40 = 0.825, prober_b 31/34 = 0.912, combined 64/74 = 0.865 as UPPER BOUND; r0104/r0105 must NOT be cited (tool defect ignored exclude_passages, r0108); prober_b duplicate-submission disclosed per r0109; leaked passage zh_16_096 exclusion verified (r0033); ID-prefix cueing never ruled out (r0107).
process_disclosures.governance: Dual-planner operator error (r0118/r0114) and credit-overage ratification path (r0117 -> r0120) disclosed; PHASE 2 budget fixed by human at 5 credits, no extension, exhausted exactly.

conclusion.limitations: Taxonomy-coding sensitivity demonstrated across runs; no drop_contested sensitivity executed in either phase (auditor condition r0148 unexecuted at 0 credits, maps to r0153 C3); permutation nulls cannot separate a construct from construct-aligned surface features and no tournament cc carries a cc-scale CI (r0152); H-W2 estimand conflates granularity with author set and its cells are unauditable (r0144); all taxonomies are constructivist impositions, not discoveries (Smith 2003; Csikszentmihalyi & Nylan 2003, adopted r0117; T_retro explicitly retrospective, r0129); cross-taxonomy ranks descriptive only; seals imperfect (zh blind readers above chance, upper bound 0.865; no en recognition probe for talkie's pre-1931 cut); citation/record defects on file (Soames DOI and Critchley ch.2 unverifiable, Mach DOI mismatch 10.1037/12902-000 vs 13802-000 with frozen label unaffected, SEP Croce placeholder, r0132 and r0158 storage gaps); small samples and wide intervals throughout (zh 20-23 testable books, en 21-25 authors; p_perm floor 0.0005). next_experiment.what: r0153 candidate C1: tournament(T_retro, talkie) restricted via exclude_units to the 12 original-English authors (3 per class), 1 credit, requires new human authorization; free companions AE2 (cc-comparability reanalysis of existing runs) and C6 (corpus_map).
next_experiment.why: Every executed PHASE 2 run is consistent with talkie keying on translation status rather than doctrine: the translation-status-only oracle ceiling (0.476) matches observed accuracy (0.483), and doctrinally central original-English Continentals sit on the floor. Only the original-English stratum can carry doctrinal signal - cc ~ 0 would prove subsumption and kill H-W1 beyond confound; cc materially > 0 with Bosanquet/Green/Royce separated from Moore/Russell/Mill would be genuine surviving doctrinal signal. Caveat pre-stated: 3 units per class, wide CI.

conclusion.overall_statement: PHASE 1: the instruments work (H-C2, replicated), the six-schools grid predicts above its own null but its claimed superiority over genre did not survive pre-registration or replication (H-C1), and the sealed-tomb 'between Dao and Fa' result is coding-dependent and did not replicate (H-C3). PHASE 2: the post-1945 analytic/continental division is NOT cleanly visible to a reader who has never heard of it - what that reader demonstrably sees is largely surface provenance (translation status, national-intellectual community), and the doctrinal question stays undecided pending C1 (H-W1); the hindsight gap was not testable as designed (H-W2). Nothing here should be relied on before the listed validations run. Agent-generated; human approval required.
